sections.title: When the answer depends on a stretch

blocks.html:
Some problems keep combining neighbours: merging files, multiplying a chain of matrices, bursting balloons, cutting a stick. Whatever you do, the final step joins a left part and a right part. So the state is a stretch i..j:

dp[i][j] = best over k of ( dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + cost of joining them )

blocks.name: ds-piles
blocks.title: Merging six files: greedy against interval DP
blocks.goal: Run greedy to the end, then run interval DP and compare the total cost.
blocks.intro: Merging two neighbouring files costs their combined size.

blocks.html: Order matters. dp[i][j] reads shorter stretches inside it, so fill by length: all stretches of length 2, then 3, and so on. (Going i from high to low and j from low to high also works.) There are O(n²) stretches and O(n) splits each: O(n³), fine for n up to a few hundred.

blocks.title: Merge cost, filled by length

blocks.code:
s = "abba"
n = len(s)
pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    for j in range(i, n):
        pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or pal[i + 1][j - 1])
print(sum(map(sum, pal)))

blocks.q: Why fill interval DP by length?

opts.t: Every stretch is built from strictly shorter stretches inside it, so those must be filled first

blocks.why: Row-by-row (i increasing) would read dp[k + 1][j] before it exists.

blocks.title: merge_cost
blocks.prompt: Merging two neighbouring piles costs their combined size; keep merging until one pile is left. Return the cheapest total. Use prefix sums for the size of a stretch and fill dp by length.
blocks.tests:
assert merge_cost([7, 3, 7, 2, 9, 9]) == 93
assert merge_cost([3, 2, 4, 1]) == 20
assert merge_cost([5]) == 0
assert merge_cost([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]) == 102
hints: The starter is the sim's greedy. In the DP the last merge joins i..k with k + 1..j, and it costs the size of the whole stretch whatever k is.
blocks.starter:
def merge_cost(piles):
    piles, cost = piles[:], 0
    while len(piles) > 1:
        k = min(range(len(piles) - 1), key=lambda k: piles[k] + piles[k + 1])
        s = piles[k] + piles[k + 1]
        cost += s
        piles[k:k + 2] = [s]
    return cost

lines: pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or pal[i + 1][j - 1])

blocks.html:
Two ways to think about k:

  • First split: the stretch is cut into i..k and k + 1..j (merging files, matrix chains).
  • Last action: k is the last thing done inside i..j. For balloons, if k bursts last, its neighbours at that moment are the edges i and j, and the two sides never interact. Thinking "first" here fails because bursting changes who is next to whom.

blocks.title: matrix_chain
blocks.prompt: The classic interview DP. Matrix t has shape dims[t] × dims[t + 1]. Multiplying a p × q by a q × r matrix costs p·q·r. Return the fewest scalar multiplications to multiply the whole chain.
blocks.tests:
assert matrix_chain([10, 30, 5, 60]) == 4500
assert matrix_chain([40, 20, 30, 10, 30]) == 26000
assert matrix_chain([10, 20]) == 0
assert matrix_chain([1, 2, 3, 4, 3]) == 30
hints: The product of matrices i..k has shape dims[i] × dims[k + 1], and k + 1..j has shape dims[k + 1] × dims[j + 1].

blocks.title: burst_balloons
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 312, a hard one asked at Google and Amazon. Bursting balloon k earns left × nums[k] × right, using its current neighbours (1 past either end). Return the most coins. Pad with 1s; dp[i][j] = best for the balloons strictly between i and j, choosing which one k bursts last.
blocks.tests:
assert max_coins([3, 1, 5, 8]) == 167
assert max_coins([1, 5]) == 10
assert max_coins([7]) == 7
assert max_coins([9, 76, 64, 21, 97, 60]) == 1086136
hints: If k is the last balloon between i and j, everything between i and k is already gone, so its neighbours are exactly a[i] and a[j].
blocks.starter:
def max_coins(nums):
    a, total = [1] + nums + [1], 0
    while len(a) > 2:
        k = min(range(1, len(a) - 1), key=lambda k: a[k])
        total += a[k - 1] * a[k] * a[k + 1]
        a.pop(k)
    return total

blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1547, a hard one asked at Google. A stick of length n must be cut at every position in cuts; each cut costs the length of the piece being cut. Return the cheapest total. Sort the cuts, add 0 and n as edges, and choose which cut happens first inside each piece.

assert min_cut_cost(9, [5, 6, 1, 4, 2]) == 22
assert min_cut_cost(5, []) == 0
assert min_cut_cost(10, [5]) == 10

blocks.starter:
def min_cut_cost(n, cuts):
    return n * len(cuts)

blocks.title: predict_the_winner
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 486, asked at Google and Amazon. Two players take turns taking a number from either end of nums; both play perfectly. Return how many points the first player wins by (first minus second; may be negative). dp[i][j] = best margin for whoever moves on nums[i..j].

blocks.title: triangulate_polygon
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1039, asked at Uber. A convex polygon's corners have values v in order. Split it into triangles; each triangle scores the product of its three corners. Return the smallest total. The edge i–j belongs to exactly one triangle (i, k, j).

def min_score(v):

blocks.q: What's the usual running time of interval DP?

opts.t: O(n³): O(n²) stretches, each trying O(n) split points

blocks.why: Fine for n in the hundreds; too slow for 10⁵.

blocks.q: In burst balloons, why choose the balloon burst last in i..j?

opts.t: Its neighbours at that moment are fixed (i and j), so the two sides are independent

blocks.why: Choosing the first one burst would change who is next to whom.

blocks.q: In matrix chain, what does the cost dims[i] · dims[k + 1] · dims[j + 1] pay for?

opts.t: Multiplying the product of matrices i..k by the product of k + 1..j

blocks.why: Shapes (dims[i] × dims[k+1]) times (dims[k+1] × dims[j+1]).

blocks.q: In "predict the winner", why is it nums[i] − dp[i + 1][j]?

opts.t: After you take nums[i], the opponent plays the rest perfectly and their margin counts against you

blocks.why: One table works for both players because it stores the margin of whoever is to move.

blocks.q: Which of these is not usually interval DP?

opts.t: Shortest path in a graph with non-negative weights

blocks.why: That's Dijkstra (chapter 23).

sections.title: Real-world project: a keyword lookup tree

blocks.title: The fastest lookup tree for a compiler's keywords
blocks.client: A language tool team whose tokenizer checks every word against a fixed list of keywords, millions of times a day, with very uneven frequencies
blocks.brief: Build obst.py. Given sorted keywords and how often each is looked up, build the binary search tree with the smallest expected cost, where a lookup costs the depth of its key (root = 1). For each stretch of keys i..j − 1, try every key r as the root: the cost is the two subtrees plus the total frequency of the stretch (everything gets one level deeper). Store the best root so you can rebuild the tree.
blocks.why: Compilers, static dictionaries and database indexes built once and read constantly benefit from this. It's also the classic interval DP that Knuth sped up to O(n²).
skills: rebuilding the tree from root choices
milestones: Record the best root per stretch
stretch: Knuth's speed-up: the best root lies between the roots of the two neighbouring stretches
Include the cost of unsuccessful searches

blocks.title: obst_cost
blocks.prompt: Return the smallest total Σ freq × depth for a BST over the keys (in the given order) with frequencies freq. Use half-open stretches: dp[i][j] for keys i..j − 1, with dp[i][i] = 0.
blocks.tests:

assert obst_cost([10, 12]) == 32
assert obst_cost([5]) == 5
assert obst_cost([4, 2, 6, 3]) == 26
hints: Making r the root pushes every other key in the stretch one level down, which adds the stretch's total frequency once.

blocks.title: obst_preorder

blocks.tests:
assert obst_preorder(["do", "if", "int"], [34, 8, 50]) == ["int", "do", "if"]
assert obst_preorder(["a", "b", "c", "d"], [4, 2, 6, 3]) == ["c", "a", "b", "d"]
assert obst_preorder(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"], [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]) == ["b", "a", "d", "c", "e"]

blocks.starter:
def obst_preorder(keys, freq):
    return [k for _, k in sorted(zip(freq, keys), reverse=True)]

blocks.q: Explain interval DP: what the state is, the split-point transition, the fill order, its running time, and the "last action" idea.
blocks.a: Interval DP solves problems where neighbours keep being combined, so the final step always joins a left part and a right part; the state dp[i][j] is the best answer for the stretch i..j. The transition tries every split point k and combines dp[i][k] and dp[k + 1][j] with the cost of joining them, such as the size of the stretch when merging files or dims[i]·dims[k + 1]·dims[j + 1] for a matrix chain. Each stretch reads strictly shorter stretches, so it is filled by length (or i decreasing with j increasing); filling rows with i increasing reads cells that are not yet computed. There are O(n²) stretches with O(n) splits each, so O(n³). When an action changes the neighbours, as in burst balloons, choose k as the last action in the stretch so its neighbours are the fixed edges and the two sides stay independent; cutting a stick chooses the first cut instead. Two-player games taking from the ends store the margin for whoever moves, nums[i] − dp[i + 1][j]. Recording the best split per stretch rebuilds the structure, such as an optimal binary search tree.

chapters.title: Bitmask DP
chapters.tagline: When the state is "which ones are used", store it in the bits of an integer
goals: Store a set of up to ~20 items as the bits of one integer
Test, add and remove items with &, | and ^
Solve assignment and tour problems over subsets in O(2ⁿ · n) or O(2ⁿ · n²)
Search (node, set) states with BFS
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import deque

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

sections.title: Remember the set, not the order

blocks.html: Some problems ask for the best order or matching of a few items: visit every shop, give each worker one job, split numbers into equal groups. Backtracking tries all n! orders. But often the future only depends on which items are already used (and maybe where you are now), not on the order you used them in. There are only 2ⁿ sets, far fewer than n!.

blocks.name: ds-tsp
blocks.title: A van, a depot and nine shops
blocks.goal: Run brute force to the end, then run Held-Karp and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Find the shortest round trip from the depot through every shop.

blocks.html:
A set of items 0..n − 1 fits in one integer: bit j is 1 if item j is in the set.

OperationCode
is j in m?m >> j & 1 (or m & (1 << j))
add j`m(1 << j)`
remove jm & ~(1 << j), or m ^ (1 << j) if it's in
size of the setbin(m).count("1")
all n items(1 << n) − 1

Held-Karp (the travelling salesperson): dp[m][last] = the shortest path that starts at the depot, visits exactly the shops in m, and ends at last. Extend it to any shop nxt not in m. Answer: min over last of dp[full][last] + d[last][depot]. That's O(2ⁿ · n²): n = 20 is about 400 million simple steps in C++, and n! for n = 20 is 2.4 × 10¹⁸.

blocks.code:
m = 0
for j in [0, 3, 4]:
    m |= 1 << j
print(bin(m), m)
print([j for j in range(6) if m >> j & 1])
print("has 3:", m >> 3 & 1, " has 2:", m >> 2 & 1)
m ^= 1 << 3
print("removed 3:", bin(m), "size", bin(m).count("1"))
print("all of 0..5:", bin((1 << 6) - 1))
blocks.title: Sets as integers

blocks.code:
m = 0b1011
subs = []
s = m
while s:
    subs.append(bin(s))
    s = (s - 1) & m
print(subs)

blocks.q: Why is (set visited, current shop) enough state for the shortest tour?

opts.t: What's left to do depends only on which shops remain and where you are, not on the order you came
Because the graph is a tree
It isn't; you need the whole path

blocks.why: Two partial routes with the same set and the same end are interchangeable, so keep the shorter.

blocks.title: assign_jobs
blocks.prompt: The assignment problem. cost[w][j] is what worker w charges for job j. Give each worker exactly one job (all different). Return the cheapest total. dp[m] = cheapest way to give jobs m to the first popcount(m) workers.
hints: The next worker to assign is the one numbered popcount(m), so the worker isn't part of the state. Greedy lets the first worker grab a job someone else needed more.
blocks.starter:
def assign(cost):
    used, total = set(), 0
    for row in cost:
        j = min((j for j in range(len(row)) if j not in used), key=lambda j: row[j])
        used.add(j)
        total += row[j]
    return total

blocks.title: membership_bug
blocks.prompt: This assignment DP tests "is job j used?" with m & j, which compares the numbers m and j bit by bit instead of looking at bit j. Job 0 always looks free, so it gets handed out again and again. Fix the test.
hints: 1 << j is the number with only bit j set. Test against that.

blocks.title: Every non-empty submask of a mask
blocks.tests:

assert submasks(0b100) == [4]
assert submasks(0) == []

blocks.html: Iterating every submask of every mask costs O(3ⁿ) in total (each item is out, in the mask only, or in both), which is fine for n ≤ 15 or so.

blocks.title: shortest_tour
blocks.prompt: Held-Karp. d is an n × n distance matrix; start and end at city 0 and visit every other city once. Return the length of the shortest tour. Use dp[m][last] over the cities 1..n − 1.
hints: The starter always drives to the nearest unvisited city: fast, often wrong (456 here). Push forward from each state: try every city not yet in m.
blocks.starter:
def tour(d):
    n, cur, seen, total = len(d), 0, {0}, 0
    while len(seen) < n:
        j = min((j for j in range(n) if j not in seen), key=lambda j: d[cur][j])
        total += d[cur][j]
        seen.add(j)
        cur = j
    return total + d[cur][0]

blocks.title: partition_k_subsets
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 698, asked at LinkedIn and Amazon. Can nums be split into k groups with equal sums? Let t = sum / k. dp[m] = the sum in the current, unfinished group after using the numbers in m (that's the total mod t), or -1 if m can't be reached. Add a number only if it fits in the current group.
blocks.tests:

assert not can_partition_k([1, 2, 3, 4], 3)
assert not can_partition_k([2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5], 4)
assert can_partition_k([1, 1, 1, 1], 2)
assert can_partition_k([10, 10, 10, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 6, 6, 6], 3)

blocks.starter:
def can_partition_k(nums, k):
    return sum(nums) % k == 0

blocks.q: What does m >> j & 1 tell you?

opts.t: The number m divided by j
Whether bit j of m is set, i.e. whether item j is in the set

blocks.why: Shift bit j down to position 0, then keep just that bit.

blocks.q: Roughly how big can n be for an O(2ⁿ · n²) bitmask DP?
blocks.why: 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶, times n² = 400 makes 4 × 10⁸.

blocks.q: In the assignment problem, why isn't the worker part of the state?

opts.t: The next worker is always number popcount(m), because workers are assigned in order
The worker is the highest bit of m

blocks.why: Fixing the order of workers removes one dimension.

blocks.q: s = (s - 1) & m repeated from s = m lists what?

opts.t: Every submask of m, from largest to smallest

blocks.why: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and everything below it; & m keeps only bits of m.

blocks.q: Why does "shortest path visiting all nodes" BFS over (node, mask) instead of nodes?

opts.t: You may revisit nodes, so the same node with a different visited set is a different state

blocks.why: The mask records progress; the node records where you are.

sections.title: Real-world project: a field technician's day

blocks.title: Plan the technician's route
blocks.client: A home-appliance repair company whose technicians visit up to a dozen customers a day from the depot

Then answer the dispatcher's other question: if the day only allows a total driving distance budget, what's the most customers that can be visited (returning to the depot)?

Two technicians splitting the customers

blocks.q: Explain bitmask DP: when the set of used items can replace the order, how sets are stored and manipulated as integers, Held-Karp and the assignment problem, and the cost and limits.
blocks.a: When the rest of a problem depends only on which items have been used (and perhaps where you are), not on the order they were used in, the state can be a set instead of a sequence: 2ⁿ sets instead of n! orders. A set of up to about 20 items is stored as an integer whose bit j says whether item j is in it: m >> j & 1 tests membership, m | 1 << j adds, m ^ 1 << j removes a member, popcount gives the size, and (1 << n) − 1 is everything. Comparing m & j instead of m & (1 << j) is a common bug. The assignment problem uses dp[m] with the next worker fixed as popcount(m), O(2ⁿ · n). Held-Karp for the shortest tour uses dp[m][last], the shortest path from the start through exactly the cities in m ending at last, extended to every city not in m, then closed back to the start: O(2ⁿ · n²), with parent pointers to rebuild the route. Partitioning into equal groups tracks the fill of the current group, (s − 1) & m enumerates submasks (O(3ⁿ) over all masks), and BFS over (node, mask) handles shortest walks that must visit every node. The limit is about n = 20.

chapters.title: DP on trees
chapters.tagline: Each node combines answers from its children
goals: Solve a tree bottom-up, one small tuple of answers per node
Choose node states such as (taken, not taken) or (covered, camera, needs cover)
Track a global best through each node for paths and diameters
Re-root a tree to get an answer for every node in O(n)

blocks.html: A tree has no cycles, so every node's subtree is its own little problem, and the subtrees of different children don't overlap. Solve the children first (post-order), then combine. The question is what each node should report to its parent: often a small tuple, one number per "situation" the parent might need.

blocks.name: ds-party
blocks.title: The company party: never invite someone with their direct boss
blocks.goal: Run greedy to the end, then run tree DP and compare the fun.
blocks.intro: Each box is a person; the number is how much fun they bring.

blocks.html:
For the party (maximum independent set on a tree), each person reports two numbers:

  • inv[v] = best for v's subtree with v invited = fun[v] + Σ out[child]
  • out[v] = best without v = Σ max(inv[child], out[child])

The answer is max(inv[root], out[root]). Each node is touched once: O(n).

Recursion depth. A tree can be a long chain: 100,000 levels deep blows Python's stack. For big trees, get a top-down order with BFS, then process it reversed (children before parents). The prelude's bfs_order does this.

blocks.code:
parent = [-1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2]
fun = [3, 2, 5, 4, 1, 6]
kids, order = bfs_order(parent)
print("top-down order:", order)
inv, out = [0] * 6, [0] * 6
for v in reversed(order):
    inv[v] = fun[v] + sum(out[c] for c in kids[v])
    out[v] = sum(max(inv[c], out[c]) for c in kids[v])
    print(f"person {v}: invited {inv[v]}, not invited {out[v]}")
print("best party:", max(inv[0], out[0]))

blocks.q: In what order are nodes processed in tree DP?

opts.t: Children before parents (post-order), so each node's children are already solved

blocks.why: Re-rooting adds a second, top-down pass after that.

blocks.q: Why use a reversed BFS order instead of recursion in Python?

opts.t: A long chain is as deep as it is long, and deep recursion overflows Python's stack

blocks.why: Reversed BFS order still puts every child before its parent.

blocks.q: For a diameter, why is there a variable outside the recursion?

opts.t: The function returns a height (what the parent needs), but the answer is a path that bends at some node, checked at every node

blocks.why: What you return and what you're looking for are different things.

blocks.q: How many states does each node report in binary tree cameras?

opts.t: 3: has a camera, watched without one, not watched yet

blocks.q: What does re-rooting give you?

opts.t: The answer with every node as the root, in O(n) total instead of O(n²)

blocks.why: Moving the root across one edge changes the answer by a formula you can apply in O(1).

blocks.client: An HR analytics startup that receives a company's org chart (each employee's manager) and builds team insights and announcement plans

Then plan an announcement: brief as few people as possible so that every employee is briefed or works directly with a briefed person (their manager or one of their direct reports). That's a minimum dominating set on a tree; it needs three states per person.
blocks.why: Org charts, file system folders (sizes), comment threads, network trees and phylogenetic trees all get analysed this way, and the charts can have hundreds of thousands of nodes, so no recursion.

Weighted version: briefing a VP costs more than briefing an intern

blocks.title: min_briefings
blocks.prompt: Return the fewest people to brief so everyone is briefed or adjacent (manager or direct report) to a briefed person. For each v keep three numbers for v's subtree: a = v is briefed; b = v isn't briefed but a direct report is (so v is covered); c = v isn't covered yet (its manager must be briefed). For b, every child takes min(a, b), and if none chose a, force the cheapest one to a. A leaf can't have b (use infinity). Answer: min(a[root], b[root]).
blocks.tests:
assert min_briefings([-1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]) == 2
assert min_briefings([-1]) == 1
assert min_briefings([-1, 0]) == 1
assert min_briefings([-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) == 2
assert min_briefings([-1, 0, 0, 0, 0]) == 1
hints: If v is briefed, its children can be in any state, even "not covered yet", because v covers them. If v relies on a child, that child must be briefed.
blocks.solution:
def min_briefings(parent):
    kids, order = bfs_order(parent)
    n = len(parent)
    INF = float("inf")
    a, b, c = [0] * n, [0] * n, [0] * n
    for v in reversed(order):
        ks = kids[v]
        a[v] = 1 + sum(min(a[k], b[k], c[k]) for k in ks)
        c[v] = sum(b[k] for k in ks)
        if ks:
            base = sum(min(a[k], b[k]) for k in ks)
            extra = min(a[k] - min(a[k], b[k]) for k in ks)
            b[v] = base + extra
        else:
            b[v] = INF
    r = order[0]
    return min(a[r], b[r])

blocks.q: Explain DP on trees: why subtrees are good subproblems, how to choose what each node reports, the global-best pattern for paths, re-rooting, and how to avoid deep recursion.
blocks.a: A tree has no cycles, so each node's subtree is an independent subproblem; solve the children first (post-order) and combine their answers at the node. The key decision is what a node reports to its parent, usually a small tuple covering each situation the parent might need: for the maximum independent set or house robber on a tree, the best with the node taken (its value plus children not taken) and without it (each child's better option), giving O(n) overall where greedy fails. Covering problems like cameras or briefing need three states: has a camera, covered without one, or not covered yet so the parent must act. For paths and diameters, a node returns the longest downward path but updates a global best by joining its two longest child paths, since the answer may bend deep inside the tree. Re-rooting computes an answer for every node as the root in O(n): a bottom-up pass gets subtree sizes and sums, then a top-down pass adjusts across each edge, such as ans[child] = ans[parent] − size[child] + (n − size[child]). In Python, long chains overflow recursion, so process a BFS order in reverse instead.

chapters.title: Digit DP
chapters.tagline: Count numbers up to 10¹⁸ by walking their digits
goals: Count numbers ≤ N with a digit property using (position, state, tight)
Explain why "tight" is needed and when it switches off
Handle leading zeros and ranges [lo, hi] with f(hi) − f(lo − 1)
Combine digit DP with masks and remainders
chapters.prelude:
import time
from functools import lru_cache

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: "How many numbers from 1 to 10¹⁸ have digit sum 90?" "How many 1s are written in all the numbers up to N?" You can't loop to 10¹⁸. But you can build the number digit by digit, from the left, and count how many ways each partial choice can be finished.

blocks.name: ds-digits
blocks.title: Numbers up to 4,327 with digit sum 13
blocks.goal: Run check every number to the end, then run digit DP and compare the work.
blocks.intro: The DP never lists a single number.

blocks.html:
While you write digits from the left, there are two situations:

  • tight: every digit so far equals the limit's digit. The next digit can only go up to the limit's next digit.
  • free: some earlier digit was smaller, so the number is already below the limit. Every later digit can be 0–9.

The template, memoised on (pos, state, tight):

`` def go(pos, state, tight): if pos == len(digits): return 1 if state is good else 0 hi = digits[pos] if tight else 9 return sum(go(pos + 1, new_state(state, d), tight and d == hi) for d in range(hi + 1)) ``

The state is whatever the property needs: a digit sum, a count of 1s, a remainder mod k, a mask of used digits. States × positions × 10 is tiny: 19 positions × 163 sums × 10 for digit sums up to 10¹⁸.

blocks.title: The template on the sim's question

blocks.q: When does tight become False?

opts.t: When the digit sum gets too big
As soon as you place a digit smaller than the limit's digit at that position
When you reach the last digit

blocks.why: Once smaller, always smaller: every later digit is free.

blocks.title: digit_sum_count
blocks.prompt: Return how many integers in [0, n] have digit sum exactly s, for n up to 10¹⁸. Memoise go(pos, sum, tight) with lru_cache; stop early when the sum passes s.
blocks.tests:
assert count_digit_sum(4327, 13) == 310
assert count_digit_sum(100, 1) == 3
assert count_digit_sum(0, 0) == 1
assert count_digit_sum(55, 10) == 5
assert count_digit_sum(10 ** 18, 90) == 24918647231083239
hints: Leading zeros are harmless here: 0042 has the same digit sum as 42.

blocks.prompt: This digit DP lets every position go up to 9, so it counts all numbers with that many digits, ignoring the limit: for n = 55, s = 10 it returns 9 (it counts 64, 73, 82 and 91 too). Add the tight flag back.
blocks.tests:
assert count_digit_sum(55, 10) == 5
assert count_digit_sum(4327, 13) == 310
assert count_digit_sum(1000, 27) == 1
hints: Start tight; the cap is the limit's digit while tight, 9 otherwise; stay tight only if you placed exactly that digit.

blocks.title: Count numbers in [0, n] that never use the digit 4
blocks.tests:
assert without_four(10) == 10
assert without_four(44) == 36
assert without_four(1000) == 730
lines: return sum(go(pos + 1, tight and d == hi) for d in range(hi + 1) if d != 4)
distractors: return sum(go(pos + 1, tight) for d in range(hi + 1) if d != 4)

blocks.html:
The state can be anything small:

  • a count (how many 1s so far)
  • a remainder (digit sum mod k, or the number itself mod k)
  • a mask of digits used (all digits distinct): 2¹⁰ masks
  • the previous digit (no two equal neighbours; no "11" in binary)
  • started (have we placed a non-zero digit yet?) when leading zeros would break the property

For a range, count f(hi) − f(lo − 1).

blocks.title: count_digit_one
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 233, a hard one asked at Google and Amazon. Return the total number of digit 1s written in all the integers from 0 to n. Carry the count of 1s so far as the state and return it at the end.
blocks.tests:
assert count_ones(13) == 6
assert count_ones(0) == 0
assert count_ones(99) == 20
assert count_ones(2023) == 1613
assert count_ones(10 ** 12) == 1200000000001
hints: The starter only counts 1s in the last position. Each finished number contributes how many 1s it used.
blocks.starter:
def count_ones(n):
    return n // 10 + (1 if n % 10 >= 1 else 0)

blocks.title: digits_from_a_set
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 902, a hard one asked at Amazon. Using only the digits in digits (strings, sorted, no 0), how many positive integers ≤ n can you write? Shorter numbers are all fine: k¹ + k² + … + k^(L−1). Then walk n's digits: count the smaller allowed digits times k^(remaining), and stop if n's digit isn't allowed. Add 1 if all of n was allowed.
hints: Here "free" has a closed form: k choices per remaining position. The tight walk ends early when the limit uses a digit you can't.
blocks.solution:
def at_most(digits, n):
    s = str(n)
    L = len(s)
    ds = sorted(int(d) for d in digits)
    k = len(ds)
    total = sum(k ** i for i in range(1, L))
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        c = int(ch)
        total += sum(1 for d in ds if d < c) * k ** (L - i - 1)
        if c not in ds:
            return total
    return total + 1

blocks.title: distinct_digit_numbers
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 2376, a hard one asked at Google. Count the integers in [1, n] whose digits are all different. The state needs a mask of used digits and a started flag: leading zeros don't count as using the digit 0.
blocks.tests:
assert count_special(20) == 19
assert count_special(5) == 5

assert count_special(1000) == 738
assert count_special(10 ** 9) == 5611770

blocks.title: no_consecutive_ones
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 600, a hard one asked at Pocket Gems. Count the integers in [0, n] whose binary form has no two adjacent 1s. Digit DP in base 2; the state is the previous bit.
blocks.tests:

assert no_adjacent_ones(10 ** 9) == 2178309

blocks.starter:
def no_adjacent_ones(n):
    return n // 2 + 1

blocks.q: Why is digit DP fast even for n = 10¹⁸?

opts.t: The state is (position, small state, tight): about 19 positions × a few hundred states × 10 digits

blocks.why: The free part only depends on how many digits are left and the state, not on which number it is.

blocks.q: How do you count numbers in [lo, hi] with some property?

opts.t: Run the DP from lo to hi
f(hi) − f(lo − 1), where f(x) counts [0, x]

blocks.why: f(lo − 1) removes everything below lo.

blocks.q: When do you need a "started" flag?

opts.t: When leading zeros would wrongly affect the property, such as "all digits distinct" or "no zero digits"

blocks.why: For a digit sum, 0042 and 42 agree, so no flag is needed.

blocks.q: What's the state for "numbers ≤ n divisible by 7"?

opts.t: The remainder of the prefix mod 7: new remainder = (r · 10 + d) % 7

blocks.why: Remainders compose digit by digit.

blocks.q: Why is the tight flag needed at all?

opts.t: While the prefix equals the limit's prefix, the next digit can't exceed the limit's digit; otherwise you'd count numbers bigger than n

blocks.why: Forgetting it counts every number with that many digits.

sections.title: Real-world project: permit numbers without unlucky digits

blocks.q: Explain digit DP: what it counts, the (position, state, tight) template, why tight is needed, leading zeros, ranges, and its cost.
blocks.a: Digit DP counts the numbers up to a huge limit N, such as 10¹⁸, that have some digit property, without listing them. It builds numbers from the left one digit at a time with a memoised function go(pos, state, tight). While tight, every digit so far equals N's digit, so the next digit can go only up to N's digit; as soon as a smaller digit is placed the number is below N and every later digit is free, 0 to 9. Forgetting tight counts every number with that many digits. The state is whatever the property needs and must stay small: a digit sum, a count of 1s, a remainder (r + d) % k or (r · 10 + d) % k, the previous digit, or a mask of used digits; a started flag stops leading zeros counting as real zeros when that matters, as for distinct digits. At the end the function returns 1 if the state is good, or the accumulated count. Ranges use f(hi) − f(lo − 1). The cost is positions × states × 10, a few thousand to a few million steps, and the free part often has a closed form, like k choices per position for a digit set.

chapters.title: Speeding up DP transitions
chapters.tagline: Same recurrence, cheaper cells
goals: Spot a transition that sums or maxes over a sliding range of earlier states
Replace a range sum with a running total or prefix sums
Replace a range max or min with a monotonic deque
Keep a "best so far" instead of rescanning
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import deque

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

sections.title: The table is right, the cells are slow

blocks.html:
Sometimes the DP is correct but too slow, because each cell looks back over a whole range:

  • ways[i] = ways[i − 1] + … + ways[i − k] costs k per cell: O(n·k)
  • best[i] = nums[i] + max(best[i − k .. i − 1]) costs k per cell
  • best[j] = max over i < j of (value[i] + i) + value[j] − j costs j per cell: O(n²)

Neighbouring cells look at almost the same range, and data structures from earlier chapters can answer "sum / max / min of this sliding range" in O(1) amortised.

blocks.name: ds-frog
blocks.title: A frog, 20 stones and jumps of up to 5
blocks.goal: Run re-add the window to the end, then run running window total and compare the operations.
blocks.intro: Each stone's count is the sum of the five stones before it.

blocks.html:
The transition reads…UseChapter
a sum over a sliding rangerunning total or prefix sums4, 8
a max/min over a sliding rangemonotonic deque12
a max/min over everything beforeone "best so far" variable–
the best earlier state with a smaller keybinary search on a sorted list31 (LIS)

Beyond this, competitive programmers use the convex hull trick, divide and conquer optimisation and Knuth's optimisation: same idea, cleverer structures.

blocks.code:
n, k, broken = 20, 5, {4, 9, 10, 15}
slow, fast = [0] * n, [0] * n
slow[0] = fast[0] = 1
window = 0
for i in range(1, n):
    slow[i] = 0 if i in broken else sum(slow[max(0, i - k):i])
    window += fast[i - 1]
    if i - k - 1 >= 0:
        window -= fast[i - k - 1]
    fast[i] = 0 if i in broken else window
print(slow == fast, fast[-1])
blocks.title: Window sums for the frog, both ways

blocks.code:
from collections import deque
vals = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2]
k, dq, out = 3, deque(), []
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    while dq and dq[0] <= i - k:
        dq.popleft()
    while dq and vals[dq[-1]] <= v:
        dq.pop()
    dq.append(i)
    out.append(vals[dq[0]])
print(out)

blocks.q: ways[i] sums the previous k cells. Moving from i to i + 1, what changes in the window?

opts.t: One cell enters (i) and one leaves (i − k)

blocks.why: Add the new cell, subtract the old one: O(1) per step.

blocks.title: frog_ways
blocks.prompt: A frog starts on stone 0 of n and jumps 1 to k stones forward; it can't land on stones in broken. Return the number of ways to reach stone n − 1, modulo 1,000,000,007. Keep a running window total instead of re-adding the window.
blocks.tests:

assert frog_ways(5, 2, []) == 5
assert frog_ways(1, 3, []) == 1
assert frog_ways(10, 3, [5]) == 58
out, t = timed(frog_ways, 20000, 300, list(range(7, 20000, 97)))
assert out == 243980156
assert t < 0.1, f"too slow: {t:.2f}s (re-adding the window?)"
hints: The starter is correct but O(n·k). Stone i − 1 enters the window for stone i, and stone i − k − 1 leaves it.
blocks.starter:
def frog_ways(n, k, broken):
    M = 10 ** 9 + 7
    b = set(broken)
    dp = [0] * n
    dp[0] = 1
    for i in range(1, n):
        s = 0
        for j in range(max(0, i - k), i):
            s += dp[j]
        dp[i] = 0 if i in b else s % M
    return dp[-1]
blocks.solution:
def frog_ways(n, k, broken):
    M = 10 ** 9 + 7
    b = set(broken)
    dp = [0] * n
    dp[0] = 1
    window = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        window = (window + dp[i - 1]) % M
        if i - k - 1 >= 0:
            window = (window - dp[i - k - 1]) % M
        dp[i] = 0 if i in b else window
    return dp[-1]

blocks.title: Jump Game VI (LeetCode 1696): DP with a monotonic deque

blocks.html:
When the transition needs the max of a sliding range, a running total won't do (you can't "subtract" a max). Keep a monotonic deque of indexes whose dp values decrease from front to back: the front is the max, anything smaller than a newcomer at the back can never win again, and indexes that fall out of range leave from the front.

When the range is "everything before me", it never shrinks, so a single variable holding the best so far is enough.

assert constrained_sum([10, -2, -10, -5, 20], 2) == 23

blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1014, asked at Wayfair and Amazon. A pair i < j scores values[i] + values[j] + i − j. Return the best score. Split it: (values[i] + i) + (values[j] − j). For each j, you only need the best values[i] + i seen so far.

def best_pair(values):
    a = sorted(range(len(values)), key=lambda i: -values[i])[:2]
    i, j = min(a), max(a)

blocks.solution:
def best_pair(values):
    best_left = values[0]
    ans = float("-inf")
    for j in range(1, len(values)):
        ans = max(ans, best_left + values[j] - j)
        best_left = max(best_left, values[j] + j)
    return ans

blocks.why: Prefix sums turn any range sum into a subtraction.

blocks.title: Cheapest hops for a delivery drone

Then output the pads the drone lands on.

blocks.title: min_hop_cost
blocks.prompt: Return the cheapest total of fees paid on pads landed on, from pad 0 to pad n − 1, jumping 1 to k pads at a time. dp[i] = fees[i] + min(dp[i − k .. i − 1]) with a deque of increasing dp values.
blocks.tests:

assert min_hop_cost([4, 1, 1, 1, 4], 1) == 11
assert min_hop_cost([0, 0], 1) == 0
assert min_hop_cost([3, 1, 50, 1, 50, 50, 1, 4], 2) == 59
assert min_hop_cost([5, 1, 8, 9, 2, 7, 3, 5], 3) == 13
hints: The starter greedily hops to the cheapest next pad, which can strand it in front of expensive ones. Flip the deque's comparison for a min.
blocks.starter:
def min_hop_cost(fees, k):
    n, i, total = len(fees), 0, fees[0]
    while i < n - 1:
        j = min(range(i + 1, min(n, i + k + 1)), key=lambda j: fees[j])
        total += fees[j]
        i = j
    return total

blocks.title: min_hop_route
blocks.prompt: Return (cost, pads) where pads lists the pads landed on, from 0 to n − 1. When you set dp[i], remember par[i] = dq[0], then walk back from n − 1.
hints: Pad 0 has no parent (-1), which ends the walk back.
blocks.starter:
def min_hop_route(fees, k):
    return sum(fees), list(range(len(fees)))
blocks.solution:
def min_hop_route(fees, k):
    n = len(fees)
    dp, par = [0] * n, [-1] * n
    dp[0] = fees[0]
    dq = deque([0])
    for i in range(1, n):
        while dq[0] < i - k:
            dq.popleft()
        dp[i] = fees[i] + dp[dq[0]]
        par[i] = dq[0]
        while dq and dp[dq[-1]] >= dp[i]:
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(i)
    pads, i = [], n - 1
    while i >= 0:
        pads.append(i)
        i = par[i]
    return dp[-1], pads[::-1]

blocks.q: Explain how to speed up a DP whose transition looks back over a range: which structure fits which transition, why the answer doesn't change, and how to recover the choices.
blocks.a: Some DPs are correct but slow because each cell scans a range of earlier cells, costing O(n·k) or O(n²). Neighbouring cells look at almost the same range, so a data structure can answer each range query in O(1) amortised while the states and recurrence stay exactly the same, giving the same table. A sum over a sliding range uses a running total (add the cell that enters, subtract the one that leaves, i − k − 1 for a window of k ending at i − 1) or prefix sums, as in counting frog jumps, dice totals or the New 21 Game probabilities, and prefix counts answer "is any index in this range reachable?". A max or min over a sliding range uses a monotonic deque of indexes, dropping indexes that leave from the front and dominated ones from the back, as in Jump Game VI and constrained subsequence sum. When the range is everything before, one best-so-far variable is enough, often after separating the terms that depend on i from those that depend on j. Recording which index produced each cell lets you walk back and recover the chosen hops. Harder versions use the convex hull trick, divide and conquer or Knuth optimisation.

chapters.title: GCD and modular arithmetic
chapters.tagline: Euclid's shortcut, and keeping huge numbers small
goals: Compute gcd and lcm in O(log n) with Euclid's algorithm
Use extended Euclid to solve a·x + b·y = c
Add, subtract and multiply modulo M without overflow or negative answers
Combine remainders with the Chinese remainder theorem
chapters.prelude:
import time
from math import gcd
from functools import reduce

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
Part 5 is the maths that shows up again and again in contests and in interviews at quant and search companies. It starts with the oldest algorithm still in daily use.

The greatest common divisor gcd(a, b) is the largest number dividing both. Picture it as the biggest square tile that covers an a × b floor exactly:

blocks.name: ds-gcd
blocks.title: Tiling a 336 × 210 floor with the biggest squares
blocks.goal: Run try every size to the end, then run Euclid and compare the steps.
blocks.intro: Any square that tiles both sides also tiles what's left after cutting squares off.

blocks.html:
Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), and gcd(a, 0) = a. Every two steps the larger number at least halves, so it's O(log n): about 90 steps for 18-digit numbers. Then:

  • lcm(a, b) = a // gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to keep numbers small in other languages)
  • gcd of a list: fold it, reduce(gcd, nums)
  • a fraction p/q in lowest terms: divide both by gcd(p, q)

Extended Euclid also finds whole numbers x, y with a·x + b·y = gcd(a, b). So a·x + b·y = c has integer solutions exactly when gcd(a, b) divides c (Bézout). That's why a 3 L and a 5 L jug can measure 4 L, but a 2 L and a 6 L jug can't measure 5 L.

blocks.title: Euclid, step by step, and extended Euclid

blocks.code:
a, b, steps = 10 ** 18, 6 * 10 ** 17 + 12, 0
while b:
    a, b = b, a % b
    steps += 1
print(a, steps)

blocks.q: Why does Euclid's algorithm take only O(log n) steps?

opts.t: After two steps the larger number is at most half what it was
Because a mod b is always 1

blocks.why: If b ≤ a/2, a mod b < b ≤ a/2; otherwise a mod b = a − b < a/2.

blocks.html:
Answers like "how many ways" grow astronomically, so problems ask for them modulo a prime, usually M = 1_000_000_007 (it's prime, and the product of two numbers below it fits in 64 bits). The rules:

  • (a + b) % M = ((a % M) + (b % M)) % M, and the same for − and ×. So reduce as you go.
  • Subtraction can go negative: write (a − b) % M. In Python % always returns a value in [0, M); in C++ and Java it doesn't, so add M first.
  • Division doesn't work this way. (a / b) % M needs the modular inverse of b (chapter 39).

def add_fractions(a, b, c, d):
    n, den = a * d + c * b, b * d
    g = gcd(n, den)
    n, den = n // g, den // g
    if den < 0:
        n, den = -n, -den
    return n, den

blocks.q: Explain Euclid's algorithm and why it is fast, extended Euclid and Bézout, and the rules for arithmetic modulo M.
blocks.a: The gcd of a and b is the largest number dividing both, like the biggest square tile covering an a × b floor. Euclid's algorithm uses gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), stopping at gcd(a, 0) = a, because any common divisor also divides the remainder; the larger number at least halves every two steps, so it is O(log n). From it, lcm(a, b) = a // gcd(a, b) · b, the gcd of a list is a fold, and fractions reduce by dividing by the gcd. Extended Euclid also returns x and y with a·x + b·y = gcd(a, b), so a·x + b·y = c has integer solutions exactly when the gcd divides c (Bézout), as in the water-jug puzzle, and the solutions shift x by b/g. Merging congruences pairwise this way is the Chinese remainder theorem. Huge counts are reported modulo a prime such as 1,000,000,007, which keeps products within 64 bits; addition, subtraction and multiplication can be reduced as you go, a difference must be reduced again so it is not negative, and division needs a modular inverse instead.

chapters.title: Primes and the sieve
chapters.tagline: Cross off multiples once, then answer prime questions instantly
goals: Test one number for primality in O(√n) with trial division
Find every prime up to n with the Sieve of Eratosthenes in O(n log log n)
Factorise many numbers fast with a smallest-prime-factor sieve
Count divisors from a prime factorisation, and sieve a window of huge numbers
chapters.prelude:
import math
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A prime has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. So 1 is not prime, 2 is the only even prime, and every whole number above 1 splits into primes in exactly one way (360 = 2·2·2·3·3·5).

To test one number n, divide by 2, 3, 4, … but only up to √n: if n = a·b, one of a and b is at most √n. That's trial division, O(√n) per number. Fine for one number near 10¹², too slow for every number up to a million:

blocks.name: ds-sieve
blocks.title: Finding the primes up to 100
blocks.goal: Run trial division to the end, then run sieve and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Trial division tests each number alone. The sieve lets each prime cross off its own multiples.

blocks.html:
The Sieve of Eratosthenes turns it round. Start with everything marked "maybe prime". Take the smallest unmarked number p: it's prime. Cross off p², p² + p, p² + 2p, …. Stop when p² > n. Whatever is left unmarked is prime.

  • Start at p²: a smaller multiple k·p with k < p was already crossed off by k's smallest prime.
  • The work is n/2 + n/3 + n/5 + … = O(n log log n), practically linear.
  • In Python, cross off with one slice assignment, s[p*p::p] = [False] * len(range(p*p, n + 1, p)). It runs in C and is about 20 times faster than a loop.

Store the smallest prime factor of every number instead of True/False, and you can factorise any number up to n in O(log n): divide by spf[x] until you reach 1.

blocks.title: Trial division, the sieve and the smallest-prime-factor table

blocks.q: Why does trial division only need to try divisors up to √n?

opts.t: If n = a·b with both factors above √n, then a·b > n, so one factor is at most √n
Because even numbers can be skipped
It doesn't: it must try up to n − 1

blocks.why: Finding no divisor up to √n means there is none at all, apart from n itself.

blocks.q: Explain trial division and why it stops at √n, how the Sieve of Eratosthenes works and why it starts at p², and how a smallest-prime-factor table factorises numbers and counts divisors.
blocks.a: A prime has exactly two divisors, so 1 is not prime. Trial division tests one number by dividing by 2, 3, … up to √n, because if n = a·b one factor is at most √n; that is O(√n) per number, fine for one number near 10¹² but too slow for every number up to a million. The Sieve of Eratosthenes marks everything as maybe prime, then each unmarked p is prime and crosses off p², p² + p, …, stopping when p² passes n; starting at p² is safe because smaller multiples k·p were already crossed off by k's smallest prime, and the total work n/2 + n/3 + n/5 + … is O(n log log n). In Python a slice assignment does the crossing in C. Storing the smallest prime factor instead of True/False lets you factorise any x up to n in O(log x) by dividing by spf[x] repeatedly, provided the table keeps the first (smallest) prime that reaches each number. With n = p₁^e₁ · p₂^e₂ · …, the number of divisors is (e₁ + 1)(e₂ + 1)…. For huge ranges, a segmented sieve sieves base primes up to √R and crosses off their multiples in the window [L, R] only.

chapters.title: Fast power and the modular inverse
chapters.tagline: Huge exponents in a handful of steps, and how to divide modulo a prime
goals: Compute a^e mod m in O(log e) by squaring and multiplying
Divide modulo a prime with Fermat's little theorem
Find an inverse modulo any m with extended Euclid, and know when none exists
Use fast power for counting problems and a toy RSA
chapters.prelude:
import time
M = 10 ** 9 + 7

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: Problems love answers like 2^(10¹⁸) mod 1,000,000,007. Multiplying one at a time takes 10¹⁸ steps. But squaring doubles the exponent: 3 → 3² → 3⁴ → 3⁸ → …. Write the exponent in binary and multiply together the powers whose bit is 1:

blocks.name: ds-fastpow
blocks.title: 3¹⁰⁰ mod 997, two ways
blocks.goal: Run multiply 100 times to the end, then run square and multiply and compare.

blocks.html:
Binary exponentiation, iteratively: keep result = 1 and base = a. While e > 0: if e is odd, result = result · base; then base = base² and e //= 2. Reduce mod m after every multiplication. It's O(log e): about 60 squarings for 10¹⁸.

In Python, pow(a, e, m) does exactly this, in C. Never write a ** e % m for a big e: it builds the whole giant number first.

Chapter 37 said division doesn't survive % M. Instead, multiply by the inverse: the b⁻¹ with b · b⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod M).

  • Fermat's little theorem: if M is prime and b isn't a multiple of it, b^(M−1) ≡ 1, so b⁻¹ = b^(M−2) mod M. One fast power.
  • So a / b mod M = a · pow(b, M − 2, M) % M. Python 3.8+ also has pow(b, -1, M).
  • If M isn't prime, use extended Euclid (chapter 37): b·x + M·y = 1 makes x the inverse. It exists only when gcd(b, M) = 1.

That's how a probability P/Q is reported "modulo 998244353": as P · Q⁻¹.

blocks.code:
def fast_pow(a, e, m):
    result, base = 1, a % m
    while e > 0:
        if e & 1:
            result = result * base % m
        base = base * base % m
        e >>= 1
    return result

print(fast_pow(3, 100, 997), pow(3, 100, 997))
print(fast_pow(2, 10 ** 18, M))

inv2 = pow(2, M - 2, M)
print(inv2, 2 * inv2 % M)
print("7 / 2 mod M =", 7 * inv2 % M)
print(pow(3, -1, 10), "because 3 × 7 = 21")

blocks.q: Explain square-and-multiply and why it is O(log e), how to divide modulo a prime, and how to find an inverse when the modulus isn't prime.
blocks.a: Multiplying a by itself e times is O(e), hopeless for e = 10¹⁸. Squaring doubles the exponent, so a, a², a⁴, a⁸, … take one multiplication each, and writing e in binary says which of those powers to multiply into the result: when the lowest bit is 1 multiply, then square the base and halve e. That is O(log e), about 60 squarings for 10¹⁸, reducing mod m after every step; Python's pow(a, e, m) does it, while a ** e % m builds a giant number first. Division does not survive reduction, so instead multiply by the inverse b⁻¹ with b·b⁻¹ ≡ 1. If M is prime, Fermat's little theorem gives b^(M−1) ≡ 1, so b⁻¹ = b^(M−2) mod M; that is how a probability P/Q is reported as P·Q⁻¹. If the modulus isn't prime, extended Euclid solves b·x + m·y = 1, and x mod m is the inverse, which exists only when gcd(b, m) = 1. RSA uses both: d = e⁻¹ mod (p − 1)(q − 1), and messages are encrypted and decrypted with fast powers.

chapters.tagline: nCr, factorial tables, stars and bars, and inclusion-exclusion
goals: Count choices with C(n, r) and Pascal's rule
Answer many C(n, r) mod p queries in O(1) with factorial and inverse-factorial tables
Turn "share out identical things" into stars and bars

chapters.prelude:
import time
from math import comb, factorial
from fractions import Fraction
M = 10 ** 9 + 7

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: Counting problems ask "how many ways" when listing them all would take longer than the universe has existed. The workhorse is C(n, r), "n choose r": the number of ways to pick r things from n when order doesn't matter.

blocks.name: ds-pascal
blocks.title: Choosing 4 friends out of 10
blocks.goal: Run list every group to the end, then run Pascal's triangle and compare.
blocks.intro: A group either includes the last friend or it doesn't. That one fact builds the whole triangle.

blocks.html:
• Pascal's rule: C(n, r) = C(n − 1, r − 1) + C(n − 1, r), with C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1. A DP table, good for n up to a few thousand.
  • The formula: C(n, r) = n! / (r! · (n − r)!). Python's math.comb gives the exact big number.
  • Modulo a prime, many queries: precompute fact[i] and inv_fact[i] up to n once, O(n). Then each C(n, r) = fact[n] · inv_fact[r] · inv_fact[n − r] mod M is O(1). Get inv_fact[n] = fact[n]^(M−2) with one fast power (chapter 39), then go down: inv_fact[i − 1] = inv_fact[i] · i.

Patterns that come back again and again:

  • Grid paths: moving right a times and down b times, choose which of the a + b moves are "right": C(a + b, a).
  • Stars and bars: share k identical sweets among n children = arrange k stars and n − 1 bars: C(k + n − 1, n − 1). If everyone must get at least one, hand those out first: C(k − 1, n − 1).
  • Catalan numbers C(2n, n) / (n + 1): valid bracket strings, binary search tree shapes, ways to triangulate a polygon.

blocks.code:
row = [1]
for n in range(6):
    print(row)
    row = [1] + [row[i] + row[i + 1] for i in range(len(row) - 1)] + [1]

N = 10 ** 6
fact = [1] * (N + 1)
for i in range(1, N + 1):
    fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % M
inv_fact = [1] * (N + 1)
inv_fact[N] = pow(fact[N], M - 2, M)
for i in range(N, 0, -1):
    inv_fact[i - 1] = inv_fact[i] * i % M

def nCr(n, r):
    if r < 0 or r > n:
        return 0
    return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % M * inv_fact[n - r] % M

print(nCr(10, 4), comb(10, 4))
print(nCr(10 ** 6, 5 * 10 ** 5))

blocks.q: Explain C(n, r) and Pascal's rule, how to answer many C(n, r) mod p queries quickly, stars and bars, and inclusion-exclusion.
blocks.a: C(n, r) counts the ways to choose r things from n when order doesn't matter. Pascal's rule C(n, r) = C(n − 1, r − 1) + C(n − 1, r) comes from looking at one item: either it is chosen, leaving r − 1 to pick from the rest, or it is not. That fills a triangle without listing any subsets. The formula n! / (r!(n − r)!) gives the same number; for many queries modulo a prime, precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to n in O(n), using one fast power for inv_fact[n] and then inv_fact[i − 1] = inv_fact[i] · i, so each query is three multiplications. Common shapes: grid paths are C(a + b, a); sharing k identical items among n people is C(k + n − 1, n − 1) by stars and bars, or C(k − 1, n − 1) if everyone needs one; Catalan numbers C(2n, n)/(n + 1) count bracket strings and BST shapes. When counting things with at least one of several properties, inclusion-exclusion adds single sets, subtracts pairs, adds triples and so on, looping over subsets with a bitmask; derangements come from the same idea.

sections.title: An integer is a row of switches

blocks.html:
Every integer is stored in binary: 13 = 1101₂ = 8 + 4 + 1. Bit i is worth 2ⁱ. Treating a number as a row of yes/no switches gives you a set of up to 64 items in one machine word, with set operations that take a single instruction.

With 12 = 1100₂ and 10 = 1010₂:

  • AND a & b, in both: 1000₂ = 8
  • OR a | b, in either: 1110₂ = 14
  • XOR a ^ b, in exactly one: 0110₂ = 6
  • shift left a << k, × 2ᵏ: 12 << 1 = 24
  • shift right a >> k, // 2ᵏ: 12 >> 2 = 3

The everyday moves:

  • Is bit i on? x >> i & 1. Turn it on: x | 1 << i. Off: x & ~(1 << i). Flip: x ^ 1 << i.
  • Clear the lowest 1: x & (x − 1). So x is a power of two exactly when x > 0 and x & (x − 1) == 0.
  • Keep only the lowest 1: x & −x (Fenwick trees use this, chapter 45).
  • Count the 1s (popcount): x.bit_count() in Python 3.10+, or bin(x).count("1").
  • All subsets of n items: for mask in range(1 << n), and item i is in when mask >> i & 1.

XOR is the star: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and order doesn't matter. Pairs cancel:

blocks.q: Explain how an integer works as a set of bits, the main bit operations and tricks, looping over subsets with masks, and why XOR finds the unpaired element.
blocks.a: An integer is a row of bits, bit i worth 2ⁱ, so one integer can store up to 64 yes/no flags. AND keeps bits in both, OR bits in either, XOR bits in exactly one, and shifts multiply or divide by powers of two. Test bit i with x >> i & 1, set it with x | 1 << i, clear it with x & ~(1 << i), flip it with x ^ 1 << i. x & (x − 1) clears the lowest 1 bit, so x > 0 with x & (x − 1) == 0 means a power of two; x & −x keeps the lowest 1; popcount counts the 1s. In Python comparisons bind tighter than &, so always bracket. Looping mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 visits every subset of n items, fine up to about n = 20. XOR satisfies x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x and ignores order, so XOR-ing a list cancels every pair and leaves the unpaired value in O(1) memory, where a tally needs a slot per value; for triples, count each bit modulo 3 instead.

chapters.title: Matrix exponentiation
chapters.tagline: Jump a recurrence 10¹⁸ steps ahead in about a hundred multiplications
goals: Write a linear recurrence as one matrix multiplication
Multiply and power matrices modulo M in O(k³ log n)
Count paths of exact length in a graph with powers of the adjacency matrix
Add constants and running sums by growing the matrix
chapters.prelude:
import time
M = 10 ** 9 + 7

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A loop like a, b = b, a + b is O(n), and contests ask for the 10¹⁸-th term. The trick: each step is a linear map, so it's a multiplication by a fixed matrix:

`` [F(n+1)] [1 1] [F(n) ] [F(n) ] = [1 0] [F(n−1)] ``

So n steps are Qⁿ with Q = [[1, 1], [1, 0]], and Qⁿ = [[F(n+1), F(n)], [F(n), F(n−1)]]. Powers square, exactly like numbers in chapter 39:

blocks.name: ds-matpow
blocks.title: F(60) mod 1000, two ways
blocks.goal: Run loop 60 steps to the end, then run square the matrix and compare.
blocks.intro: 60 = 32 + 16 + 8 + 4, so Q⁶⁰ = Q³² · Q¹⁶ · Q⁸ · Q⁴.

blocks.html:
The recipe for any recurrence that adds up fixed multiples of the last k terms:

  1. State vector: the last k values, like (T(n), T(n−1), T(n−2)) for Tribonacci.
  2. Transition matrix: row i says how the new i-th value is built from the old ones.
  3. Power it: Tⁿ by square-and-multiply, starting from the identity matrix. Each product of k × k matrices is k³ multiplications, so it's O(k³ log n).
  4. Reduce mod M inside every product.

Two upgrades:

  • Graphs: if A is the adjacency matrix, (Aᴸ)[u][v] counts the walks of exactly L edges from u to v.
  • Constants and running sums: add a coordinate that's always 1 (for + c), or one that accumulates (for "the total so far"). The matrix grows by one row and column.

blocks.code:
def mat_mult(a, b):
    n, k, p = len(a), len(b), len(b[0])
    return [[sum(a[i][t] * b[t][j] for t in range(k)) % M for j in range(p)] for i in range(n)]

def mat_pow(a, e):
    n = len(a)
    r = [[int(i == j) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    while e:
        if e & 1:
            r = mat_mult(r, a)
        a = mat_mult(a, a)
        e >>= 1
    return r

Q = [[1, 1], [1, 0]]
print(mat_pow(Q, 10))
fib, t = timed(lambda n: mat_pow(Q, n)[0][1], 10 ** 18)
print("F(10^18) mod M =", fib, "in", round(t * 1000, 2), "ms")

blocks.q: Explain how matrix exponentiation computes the n-th term of a linear recurrence, its cost, and how it counts walks in a graph and handles constants or running sums.
blocks.a: A recurrence that adds fixed multiples of the last k terms is one multiplication of a k × k matrix with the state vector of the last k values; for Fibonacci, Q = [[1, 1], [1, 0]] maps (F(n), F(n−1)) to (F(n+1), F(n)), and Qⁿ holds F(n) in its top-right corner. So n steps are the n-th power of one matrix, which square-and-multiply computes from the identity in log n products, reducing mod M inside each; with k³ work per product that is O(k³ log n), about a hundred products for n = 10¹⁸ instead of 10¹⁸ loop steps. The adjacency matrix A of a graph gives the number of walks of exactly L edges from u to v as (Aᴸ)[u][v]. A constant term is handled by adding a state coordinate that is always 1, and a running total by adding a coordinate that accumulates; each costs one extra row and column. Products of terms are not linear and do not fit.

chapters.title: Segment trees
chapters.tagline: Range queries and updates, both in O(log n)
goals: Explain why prefix sums fail when the array changes
Build an iterative segment tree for sum, min, max or gcd
Answer a range query and a point update in O(log n)
Store a custom summary in each node, and walk the tree to find the k-th item
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

def lcg(n, seed, mx):
    out, x = [], seed
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2 ** 31
        out.append(x % mx)
    return out

blocks.html:
Part 6 is about answering questions about ranges: sums, minimums and counts inside [l, r], and later, patterns inside strings.

Prefix sums (chapter 4) answer "sum of l..r" in O(1), but only while the array doesn't change: one update shifts every prefix after it, O(n). With 10⁵ updates and 10⁵ queries mixed together, both the naive loop and prefix sums cost about 10¹⁰.

A segment tree keeps the sum of every aligned block: each pair, each four, each eight, up to the whole array.

blocks.name: ds-segtree
blocks.title: Eight range jobs on 16 numbers
blocks.goal: Run cell by cell to the end, then run segment tree and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Any range is a few whole blocks glued together. An update touches one block per level.

blocks.html:
The iterative version is short and fast in Python. Put the leaves at t[n..2n−1], and node i is the sum of nodes 2i and 2i + 1:

  • Build: for i from n − 1 down to 1: t[i] = t[2i] + t[2i + 1]. O(n).
  • Update position p: set t[p + n], then walk up: p //= 2 and recompute, until the root. O(log n).
  • Query [l, r): start l += n, r += n. While l < r: if l is odd, take t[l] and l += 1; if r is odd, r −= 1 and take t[r]; then halve both. O(log n).

Any associative operation works: sum, min, max, gcd, product mod M, even a custom summary. Use the right "empty" value: 0 for sum, inf for min.

blocks.code:
class SegTree:
    def __init__(self, a):
        self.n = len(a)
        self.t = [0] * self.n + list(a)
        for i in range(self.n - 1, 0, -1):
            self.t[i] = self.t[2 * i] + self.t[2 * i + 1]

    def update(self, p, value):
        p += self.n
        self.t[p] = value
        while p > 1:
            p //= 2
            self.t[p] = self.t[2 * p] + self.t[2 * p + 1]

    def query(self, l, r):          # sum of a[l..r], inclusive
        res, l, r = 0, l + self.n, r + self.n + 1
        while l < r:
            if l & 1:
                res += self.t[l]
                l += 1
            if r & 1:
                r -= 1
                res += self.t[r]
            l //= 2
            r //= 2
        return res

st = SegTree([5, 3, 8, 6, 1, 4, 7, 2])
print(st.query(1, 6), st.query(0, 7))
st.update(3, 100)
print(st.query(1, 6))

blocks.title: The best trade in any window
blocks.client: A trading-desk dashboard that shows, for any time window a trader drags across a chart of prices that keep getting corrected, the high, and the best single buy-then-sell profit
blocks.brief: Build desk.py. Prices arrive per minute and late corrections overwrite old minutes. For any window [l, r] you need the highest price, and the best profit from buying at one minute and selling at a later one inside the window. The high is a max tree. The best trade needs a custom node: (lowest, highest, best). Merging a left block A with a right block B gives (min(A.low, B.low), max(A.high, B.high), max(A.best, B.best, B.high − A.low)): either the trade sits inside one half, or it buys in the left and sells in the right. Order matters, so the query collects a left result and a right result separately.

blocks.q: Explain why prefix sums fail with updates, how an iterative segment tree is laid out, how its update and query work and why they are O(log n), and how custom nodes extend it.
blocks.a: Prefix sums answer static range sums in O(1), but one update changes every prefix after it, O(n). A segment tree stores the combined value of every aligned block of 1, 2, 4, 8, … cells: in the iterative layout the leaves sit at t[n..2n−1] and node i is op(t[2i], t[2i + 1]), built bottom-up in O(n) with 2n memory. An update writes the leaf and walks up through the parents, one per level, recomputing each. A query on [l, r) moves l and r up level by level, taking t[l] when l is a right child and t[r − 1] when r is, so it combines at most about two blocks per level. Both are O(log n). Any associative operation works, such as sum, min, max or gcd, with a matching empty value; a custom node like (low, high, best) needs an order-preserving query with separate left and right results. A count tree can also be walked from the root to find the k-th present item.

chapters.title: Lazy propagation
chapters.tagline: Update a whole range in O(log n) by leaving notes
goals: Explain why range updates break a plain segment tree
Add a lazy tag to each node and push it down only when needed
Handle range add, range assign and range flip, with sum or max queries
Choose a difference array when queries only come at the end
chapters.prelude:
import sys
import time
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

def lcg(n, seed, mx):
    out, x = [], seed
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2 ** 31
        out.append(x % mx)
    return out

blocks.html:
Chapter 43's tree updates one position in O(log n). "Add 3 to every position from 2 to 13" would be 12 separate updates: O(n log n) per job, worse than a plain loop.

The fix is to be lazy. When a block lies wholly inside the update range, fix its total at once (sum += v × size) and leave a note on it: "every cell below me owes +v". Don't touch the children. Later, when a job needs to look inside that block, push the note down one level first.

blocks.name: ds-lazy
blocks.title: Range additions and range sums on 16 numbers
blocks.goal: Run touch every cell to the end, then run lazy segment tree and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Red notes are debts owed to the cells below. They're only paid when someone looks inside.

blocks.html:
The recursive version is the clearest. Node x covers [lo, hi], and its children are 2x (left half) and 2x + 1 (right half). Use arrays of size 4n:

  • apply(x, v): s[x] += v × (hi − lo + 1), lz[x] += v. The block is now right, and the note remembers the debt.
  • push(x): if lz[x] is non-zero, apply it to both children and clear it.
  • update / query: if the node is outside the range, stop. If it's wholly inside, apply (or return s[x]). Otherwise push(x), recurse into both children, and (for an update) recompute s[x].

Both are O(log n), because only the two edges of the range are ever partial at each level.

The tag changes with the job: assign needs "set to v" (a newer assign replaces an older one), flip needs "invert" (two flips cancel), and add with max just adds v to the max. If all the updates come before all the queries, you don't need a tree at all: a difference array (chapter 4) does it in O(n + q).

blocks.title: my_calendar_iii
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 732, a hard one asked at Google. Events [start, end) arrive one by one (times up to 10⁹). After each, return the largest number of events overlapping at any moment so far. Compress all the times to indices, then each event is "add 1 on [idx(start), idx(end) − 1]" and the answer is the tree's overall maximum. A neat trick for add + max: keep mx[x] = max(children) + lz[x] and never push at all.
hints: The starter only checks overlaps at the new event's start, but the busiest moment can be at an older event's start. Count over the whole timeline with range adds.
blocks.starter:
def calendar(events):
    out, best = [], 0
    for i, (s, e) in enumerate(events):
        c = sum(1 for s2, e2 in events[:i + 1] if s2 <= s < e2)
        best = max(best, c)
        out.append(best)
    return out
blocks.solution:
def calendar(events):
    xs = sorted({t for ev in events for t in ev})
    idx = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(xs)}
    n = len(xs)
    mx, lz = [0] * (4 * n), [0] * (4 * n)
    def add(x, lo, hi, l, r):
        if r < lo or hi < l:
            return
        if l <= lo and hi <= r:
            mx[x] += 1
            lz[x] += 1
            return
        m = (lo + hi) // 2
        add(2 * x, lo, m, l, r)
        add(2 * x + 1, m + 1, hi, l, r)
        mx[x] = max(mx[2 * x], mx[2 * x + 1]) + lz[x]
    out = []
    for s, e in events:
        add(1, 0, n - 1, idx[s], idx[e] - 1)
        out.append(mx[1])
    return out

blocks.solution:
def final_salaries(salaries, raises):
    n = len(salaries)
    d = [0] * (n + 1)
    for l, r, v in raises:
        d[l] += v
        d[r + 1] -= v
    out, run = [], 0
    for i in range(n):
        run += d[i]
        out.append(salaries[i] + run)
    return out

blocks.q: Explain lazy propagation: why range updates need it, what apply and push do, why it stays O(log n), and how the tag changes for add, assign and flip, plus when a difference array is enough.
blocks.a: A plain segment tree updates one position at a time, so adding to a range costs O(n log n). With lazy propagation each node keeps its value and a tag. When an update fully covers a node's block, apply fixes the node at once (sum += v × size, or max += v) and records the tag, without visiting the children. Push hands a node's tag to both children and clears it, and it runs only when a later update or query needs to go inside that block. Only the blocks at the two edges of a range are partly covered at each level, so updates and queries both touch O(log n) nodes; recursive trees use arrays of size 4n. Range add accumulates tags, range assign replaces them (with None meaning empty, since 0 is a valid value), and range flip toggles a flag and turns a count of ones into size minus that count. If all updates come before all queries, a difference array with a running sum does the job in O(n + q).

chapters.title: Fenwick trees
chapters.tagline: Prefix sums that survive updates, in one array and two tiny loops
goals: Explain what box i of a Fenwick tree holds, using the lowest set bit i & -i
Write add and prefix as two short loops, both O(log n)
Count inversions and "smaller after self" by sweeping with a Fenwick tree over values
Turn range add + point query into point add + prefix sum, and find the k-th item by descending the tree
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

def lcg(n, seed, mx):
    out, x = [], seed
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2 ** 31
        out.append(x % mx)
    return out

sections.title: Two bad choices and a good one

blocks.html:
You have numbers that change, and you keep asking "what's the sum of the first i?". The two obvious stores each lose at one job:

  • A plain array updates in one step, but a prefix sum reads up to n cells.
  • A prefix-sum array (chapter 4) answers in one step, but one update rewrites up to n totals.

A Fenwick tree (also called a binary indexed tree, or BIT) sits in between. It's one array t[1..n] where box i holds the sum of the last i & -i cells ending at i. i & -i is the lowest set bit of i: box 12 (1100) covers 4 cells, 9..12; box 8 (1000) covers 8 cells, 1..8; box 7 (0111) covers just cell 7.

blocks.name: ds-fenwick
blocks.title: Sums and updates on 16 numbers
blocks.goal: Run plain array to the end, then run Fenwick tree and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Click any blue box to see which cells it covers and why.

blocks.html:
Two loops do everything, and they mirror each other:

  • prefix(i): add t[i], then drop the lowest bit (i -= i & -i) and repeat until i is 0. 13 = 1101 visits boxes 13, 12, 8: cells 13, 9..12 and 1..8. One box per set bit, so at most log₂ n + 1.
  • add(i, v): add v to t[i], then add the lowest bit (i += i & -i) and repeat while i ≤ n. That climbs through exactly the boxes whose range covers i.

A range sum is prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1). The tree is 1-indexed because box 0 would have lowbit 0 and the loops would never move, so a 0-indexed API just adds 1 on the way in.

Compared with chapter 43's segment tree, a Fenwick tree is shorter, faster and uses n + 1 numbers instead of 4n. It can't do everything a segment tree does (minimum over an arbitrary range is awkward), but any job that's "sums of something, with updates" fits.

blocks.code:
class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.t = [0] * (n + 1)

    def add(self, i, v):          # position i is 0-indexed
        i += 1
        while i <= self.n:
            self.t[i] += v
            i += i & -i

    def prefix(self, i):          # sum of the first i numbers
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.t[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return s

f = Fenwick(8)
for i, v in enumerate([5, 3, 8, 6, 1, 4, 7, 2]):
    f.add(i, v)
print(f.t)
print(f.prefix(4), f.prefix(8), f.prefix(6) - f.prefix(2))
f.add(2, 10)
print(f.prefix(4), f.prefix(8))

blocks.code:
for i in [12, 7, 8, 13]:

blocks.why: Drop the lowest bit each time: 1011 → 1010 → 1000 → 0. Box 11 covers cell 11, box 10 covers 9..10, box 8 covers 1..8.

range_sum(l, r) is prefix(r + 1) − prefix(l) once prefix(i) means "the first i numbers".

blocks.title: count_smaller_after_self
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 315, a hard one asked at Google and Amazon. For each nums[i], count how many numbers to its right are strictly smaller. Sweep from the right, keeping a Fenwick tree over the values you've seen (compress them to ranks 1..m first). For each number, ask "how many seen values have a smaller rank?", then add it. 100,000 numbers.
blocks.tests:
assert count_smaller([5, 2, 6, 1]) == [2, 1, 1, 0]
assert count_smaller([-1, -1]) == [0, 0]
assert count_smaller([2, 0, 1]) == [2, 0, 0]
cs = count_smaller([x - 50000 for x in lcg(100000, 13, 100000)])
assert sum(cs) == 2497082015 and cs[0] == 8630 and cs[500] == 16646
hints: The starter only looks 49 places ahead. A Fenwick tree indexed by value rank counts, in O(log n), how many seen numbers are below the current one.
Ask with prefix(rank − 1) so equal values don't count, then add(rank, 1).
blocks.solution:
def count_smaller(nums):
    vals = sorted(set(nums))
    rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(vals)}
    m = len(vals)
    t = [0] * (m + 1)
    out = [0] * len(nums)
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1, -1, -1):
        r = rank[nums[i]] - 1
        s = 0
        while r > 0:
            s += t[r]
            r -= r & -r
        out[i] = s
        r = rank[nums[i]]
        while r <= m:
            t[r] += 1
            r += r & -r
    return out

blocks.title: count_inversions
blocks.prompt: A Codeforces staple. An inversion is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]. Count them for 100,000 numbers up to 10⁹. Sweep left to right: before adding a[j], the number of earlier values greater than it is j − (how many earlier values are ≤ a[j]).
blocks.tests:
assert inversions([3, 1, 2]) == 2
assert inversions([2, 4, 1, 3, 5]) == 3
assert inversions(list(range(10, 0, -1))) == 45
assert inversions([7, 7, 7]) == 0, "equal values are not inversions"
assert inversions(lcg(100000, 17, 10 ** 9)) == 2495500853
hints: The starter only counts neighbours. Every earlier value bigger than x makes one pair with it.
blocks.starter:
def inversions(a):
    return sum(1 for i in range(len(a) - 1) if a[i] > a[i + 1])
blocks.solution:
def inversions(a):
    vals = sorted(set(a))
    rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(vals)}
    m = len(vals)
    t = [0] * (m + 1)
    inv = 0
    for seen, x in enumerate(a):
        r = rank[x]
        s = 0
        while r > 0:
            s += t[r]
            r -= r & -r
        inv += seen - s
        r = rank[x]
        while r <= m:
            t[r] += 1
            r += r & -r
    return inv

Keep a Fenwick tree over the difference array (chapter 4): a range add is two point adds, at l and r + 1, and the value at i is the prefix sum up to i.

blocks.q: Why is a Fenwick tree 1-indexed?

opts.t: 0 & -0 is 0, so a loop starting at box 0 would never move

blocks.why: Every hop adds or removes the lowest set bit, and 0 has none.

blocks.q: A job asks for the minimum of any range a[l..r], with point updates. Fenwick or segment tree?

opts.t: Segment tree: a Fenwick tree answers prefixes, and you can't "subtract" a minimum to get a middle range
Neither: use a prefix minimum array

blocks.why: Sums can be subtracted: prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1). Minimums can't, which is why sums (and XOR, counts) are a Fenwick tree's home.

blocks.q: How much memory does a Fenwick tree on n numbers use?
blocks.why: One box per position, plus the unused box 0. A recursive segment tree needs about 4n.

blocks.q: In "count smaller after self", what is the Fenwick tree indexed by?

opts.t: The value's rank after sorting the distinct values

blocks.why: You're asking "how many of the numbers seen so far are below x?", which is a prefix sum over values.

blocks.title: Live ranks for a million players
blocks.client: A mobile game whose players want to see "you're rank 18,204 of 100,000" the moment a match ends, and whose weekly prize goes to whoever sits at rank 1,000
blocks.brief: Build board.py. Scores are whole numbers from 0 to top. Keep a Fenwick tree where box i counts players with each score: adding a player is add(score, 1), removing one is add(score, −1), and "how many players have at most x?" is a prefix sum. Then find the k-th lowest score without a binary search over prefix sums: start at position 0 and try steps of 2ᵏ, 2ᵏ⁻¹, … 1. Take a step whenever the box you'd land on holds fewer than k players, subtracting what it holds from k. Each step reads one box, so it's O(log n), not O(log² n).
blocks.why: Order-statistic counters like this run game leaderboards, percentile latency dashboards, and "you beat 83% of players" badges, where scores change all the time.
