blocks.starter:
class BIT:
    pass

blocks.q: Explain a Fenwick tree: what box i holds, how prefix and add walk the tree, why both are O(log n), why it's 1-indexed, and three jobs it solves beyond plain range sums.
blocks.a: A Fenwick tree is an array t[1..n] where box i holds the sum of the last i & -i cells ending at i, and i & -i is the lowest set bit of i. prefix(i) adds t[i] and drops the lowest bit (i -= i & -i) until i is 0, visiting one box per set bit. add(i, v) adds v to t[i] and adds the lowest bit (i += i & -i) while i ≤ n, visiting every box whose range covers i. Both take at most log₂ n + 1 steps, and a range sum is prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1). It's 1-indexed because 0 has no lowest bit, so the loops would never move. It uses n + 1 numbers and can be built in O(n) by passing each box's total to j + (j & -j). Beyond range sums: counting inversions or "smaller after self" with a tree over value ranks; range add with point query by keeping a tree over the difference array; and finding the k-th item by descending with powers of two. It suits sums, counts and XOR, not minimums, because those can't be subtracted.

chapters.title: Sparse tables
chapters.tagline: Build once in n log n, then answer every range minimum in two reads
goals: Build a table of minimums over every power-of-two block
Answer a range minimum with two overlapping blocks in O(1)
Explain which operations allow overlap (min, max, gcd) and which don't (sum)
Pair a sparse table with two pointers when the array never changes
chapters.prelude:
import time
from math import gcd

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

def lcg(n, seed, mx):
    out, x = [], seed
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2 ** 31
        out.append(x % mx)
    return out

def walk(n, seed, step, start):
    """A random walk: each value is the last one plus something in -step..step."""
    out, v = [], start
    for d in lcg(n, seed, 2 * step + 1):
        v += d - step
        out.append(v)
    return out

blocks.html:
Segment trees and Fenwick trees pay O(log n) per question so that the numbers can change. Very often they don't: a day of stock prices, a fixed array in a contest, the depths of an Euler tour (next chapter). Then you can do better.

A sparse table stores, for every start i and every power of two 2ᵏ, the minimum of the block a[i .. i + 2ᵏ − 1]. Row 0 is the array. Each row comes from the one below: a block of 2ᵏ is two blocks of 2ᵏ⁻¹ side by side.

blocks.name: ds-sparse
blocks.title: Range minimums on 16 numbers
blocks.goal: Run scan the range to the end, then run sparse table and compare the reads.
blocks.intro: The rows above the numbers are the table: row 2^k holds the minimum of each block of 2^k.

blocks.html:
To answer min(a[l..r]), let k be the biggest power with 2ᵏ ≤ length. Two blocks of that size, one starting at l and one ending at r, cover the whole range. They usually overlap in the middle, and that's fine: min(x, x) = x, so a number counted twice changes nothing.

That gives you a rule for when a sparse table works. The operation must be idempotent (doing it twice is the same as once): min, max, gcd, bitwise AND and OR. Sum is not: an overlapping cell would be added twice. For sums of a fixed array you already have prefix sums.

k comes from (r − l + 1).bit_length() − 1, which is ⌊log₂ length⌋ without any floating point.

blocks.title: range_gcd
blocks.prompt: A Codeforces classic. Answer many questions "what's the gcd of a[l..r]?". gcd is idempotent (gcd(x, x) = x), so overlapping blocks are fine. 100,000 numbers and 100,000 questions.
hints: Same table as for minimums, with gcd in place of min.
blocks.starter:
def range_gcds(a, qs):
    return [gcd(a[l], a[r]) for l, r in qs]
blocks.solution:
def range_gcds(a, qs):
    sp = [list(a)]
    k = 1
    while (1 << k) <= len(a):
        p, h = sp[-1], 1 << (k - 1)
        sp.append([gcd(p[i], p[i + h]) for i in range(len(a) - (1 << k) + 1)])
        k += 1
    out = []
    for l, r in qs:
        k = (r - l + 1).bit_length() - 1
        out.append(gcd(sp[k][l], sp[k][r - (1 << k) + 1]))
    return out

blocks.q: Why can't a sparse table answer range sums in O(1)?

opts.t: Sums are too big to store
The two blocks overlap, and the overlapping cells would be added twice
Sums need a Fenwick tree by law
It can, with a bigger table

blocks.why: min, max and gcd don't care about counting a cell twice. Sum does. (For a fixed array, prefix sums answer sums in O(1) anyway.)

blocks.q: How many numbers does a sparse table on n = 1,000,000 store, roughly?
blocks.why: 20 rows, each nearly n long. That's the price of O(1) questions: memory, and no updates.

blocks.q: One value in the array changes. What does a sparse table need?

opts.t: O(log n) fixes, like a segment tree
Every block containing it changes, so in practice you rebuild

blocks.why: A position sits in up to 2ᵏ blocks of row k. Sparse tables are for arrays that don't change.

blocks.q: For which operation is a sparse table not suitable?
blocks.why: Product isn't idempotent: a cell in the overlap would be multiplied in twice.

sections.title: Real-world project: a stock chart's zoom

blocks.title: Highs and lows at any zoom
blocks.client: A trading app whose chart shows the day's high and low for whatever window the user drags across, and flags the most volatile stretch of each length

Then find the biggest swing (high − low) among all windows of exactly w prices: there are n − w + 1 windows and each one is two O(1) questions, so the whole scan is O(n) after the build. Only build the rows you need: for a fixed w, rows up to ⌊log₂ w⌋.

blocks.title: chart_drag
blocks.prompt: Write price_range(prices, qs): for each (l, r) in qs, return (low, high) of prices[l..r]. 100,000 prices and 100,000 drags.
hints: Two tables, one with min and one with max, and the same two blocks for both.
blocks.starter:
def price_range(prices, qs):
    return [(prices[l], prices[r]) for l, r in qs]
blocks.solution:
def price_range(prices, qs):
    n = len(prices)
    lo, hi = [list(prices)], [list(prices)]
    k = 1
    while (1 << k) <= n:
        h, a, b = 1 << (k - 1), lo[-1], hi[-1]
        lo.append([min(a[i], a[i + h]) for i in range(n - (1 << k) + 1)])
        hi.append([max(b[i], b[i + h]) for i in range(n - (1 << k) + 1)])
        k += 1
    out = []
    for l, r in qs:
        k = (r - l + 1).bit_length() - 1
        j = r - (1 << k) + 1
        out.append((min(lo[k][l], lo[k][j]), max(hi[k][l], hi[k][j])))
    return out

blocks.starter:
def biggest_swing(prices, w):
    return max(prices[:w]) - min(prices[:w])
blocks.solution:
def biggest_swing(prices, w):
    n = len(prices)
    lo, hi = [list(prices)], [list(prices)]
    k = 1
    while (1 << k) <= w:
        h, a, b = 1 << (k - 1), lo[-1], hi[-1]
        lo.append([min(a[i], a[i + h]) for i in range(n - (1 << k) + 1)])
        hi.append([max(b[i], b[i + h]) for i in range(n - (1 << k) + 1)])
        k += 1
    k = w.bit_length() - 1
    best = 0
    for l in range(n - w + 1):
        j = l + w - (1 << k)
        best = max(best, max(hi[k][l], hi[k][j]) - min(lo[k][l], lo[k][j]))
    return best

blocks.q: Explain a sparse table: what it stores, how it's built, how a question is answered in O(1), which operations it works for and why, and when you'd pick it over a segment tree.
blocks.a: A sparse table stores, for every start i and every power of two 2ᵏ, the answer for the block a[i..i + 2ᵏ − 1]. Row 0 is the array, and row k comes from row k − 1, because a block of 2ᵏ is two blocks of 2ᵏ⁻¹ side by side, so building costs O(n log n) time and memory. For a question on l..r, take k = ⌊log₂(r − l + 1)⌋ (bit_length − 1) and combine the block starting at l with the block ending at r. Together they cover the range, possibly overlapping. Overlap is only harmless for idempotent operations, where applying a value twice changes nothing: min, max, gcd, AND and OR. Sum and product would count the overlap twice. Pick a sparse table when the array never changes and there are many questions, because it gives O(1) per question. If values change, use a segment tree (O(log n) updates and questions), because one change would force a rebuild.

chapters.title: LCA with binary lifting
chapters.tagline: Store every node's 1st, 2nd, 4th, 8th… ancestor, and any climb takes log n jumps
goals: Build the jump table up[k][v], the 2ᵏ-th ancestor of v, in O(n log n)
Find the k-th ancestor with one jump per set bit of k
Find the lowest common ancestor by levelling depths, then jumping both nodes from the top power down
Carry extra facts along each jump (distance, the heaviest edge) to answer path questions
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

def lcg(n, seed, mx):
    out, x = [], seed
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2 ** 31
        out.append(x % mx)
    return out

def tall_tree(n, seed):
    """A tree on 0..n-1 given as parent[v], with parent[0] = -1 and parent[v] < v. About n/2 deep."""
    g = lcg(n, seed, 3)
    return [-1] + [max(0, i - 1 - g[i]) for i in range(1, n)]

blocks.html:
Root a tree. The lowest common ancestor (LCA) of u and v is the deepest node that's an ancestor of both, the spot where their paths up to the root join. It answers a surprising number of questions:

  • the distance between two nodes is depth[u] + depth[v] − 2·depth[lca]
  • in git, merge-base is the LCA of two commits
  • in an org chart, it's the lowest manager both people report to

The obvious way is to climb: step the deeper node up until both are at the same depth, then step both up together until they meet. That's O(depth) per question, and a tree can be a long path, so O(n).

blocks.name: ds-lift
blocks.title: Five questions on a tall tree
blocks.goal: Run walk up one step at a time to the end, then run binary lifting and compare.
blocks.intro: Click a node to see its jump table: its ancestors 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 levels up.

blocks.html:
Binary lifting stores up[k][v], the ancestor 2ᵏ levels above v. Row 0 is the parent. Each row comes from the one before: going up 2ᵏ is going up 2ᵏ⁻¹ twice, so up[k][v] = up[k−1][ up[k−1][v] ]. Ancestors past the root stay at the root.

With the table:

  1. Level the depths. If u is d levels deeper, jump u up by d, one jump per set bit (d = 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 is three jumps).
  2. If they're now equal, that's the answer.
  3. Jump together, biggest power first. For k from high to low, if up[k][u] ≠ up[k][v], jump both. A jump that lands on the same node might overshoot the LCA, so you skip it. At the end u and v are just below the LCA, so the answer is up[0][u].

Both phases take O(log n) jumps. The table costs O(n log n) time and memory.

blocks.code:
class LCA:
    def __init__(self, parent):
        n = len(parent)
        self.LOG = max(1, n.bit_length())
        self.depth = [0] * n
        for v in range(1, n):                    # parent[v] < v, so parents come first
            self.depth[v] = self.depth[parent[v]] + 1
        self.up = [[p if p >= 0 else 0 for p in parent]]
        for k in range(1, self.LOG):
            prev = self.up[-1]
            self.up.append([prev[prev[v]] for v in range(n)])

    def lca(self, u, v):
        if self.depth[u] < self.depth[v]:
            u, v = v, u
        d, k = self.depth[u] - self.depth[v], 0
        while d:
            if d & 1:
                u = self.up[k][u]
            d >>= 1
            k += 1
        if u == v:
            return u
        for k in range(self.LOG - 1, -1, -1):
            if self.up[k][u] != self.up[k][v]:
                u, v = self.up[k][u], self.up[k][v]
        return self.up[0][u]

#        0
#      /   \
#     1     2
#    / \     \
#   3   4     5
#      / \
#     6   7
t = LCA([-1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 4])
print(t.up)
print(t.lca(6, 7), t.lca(3, 7), t.lca(5, 6), t.lca(6, 6))

blocks.q: In the second phase, why skip a jump that lands both nodes on the same ancestor?

opts.t: That ancestor is common, but it might be above the lowest one; only jumps that keep them apart are safe

blocks.why: Jumping to a common ancestor could overshoot. Staying just below the meeting point and then taking one parent step never does.

blocks.q: Explain binary lifting for the lowest common ancestor: what the table stores and how it's built, how to level two depths, why the second phase goes from the biggest jump down and skips jumps that land on the same node, the costs, and two path questions it answers.
blocks.a: Binary lifting stores up[k][v], the ancestor 2ᵏ levels above v. Row 0 is the parent (the root points to itself), and up[k][v] = up[k−1][up[k−1][v]], because going up 2ᵏ is going up 2ᵏ⁻¹ twice. That's O(n log n) time and memory. For lca(u, v), first lift the deeper node by the depth gap, one jump per set bit, and if they're now the same node that's the answer. Otherwise try k from the highest power down and jump both nodes only when up[k][u] ≠ up[k][v]. A jump to the same node is a common ancestor that might be above the lowest one, so skipping it never overshoots. Going from big to small is like reading a number's bits from the top. Afterwards both nodes sit just below the LCA, so it's their parent. Each question takes O(log n) jumps. With dist[v] from the root, the distance between a and b is dist[a] + dist[b] − 2·dist[lca]. Storing the heaviest edge alongside each jump answers "the heaviest edge on a path" the same way. The k-th ancestor also takes one jump per set bit of k.

chapters.title: KMP and the Z-function
chapters.tagline: Find a pattern without ever reading the text backwards
goals: Build the prefix function (KMP's failure table): the longest border of every prefix
Search a text in O(n + m) by falling back through the table after a mismatch
Build the Z-function and search with pattern + separator + text
Use borders for periods, repeats and palindromes

blocks.html:
text.find(pattern) looks easy: try every start, compare letter by letter, stop at the first mismatch. Usually that's fast. But on a text like aaaa…ab and a pattern aaa…ab, every start matches almost the whole pattern before failing. That's n × m comparisons, 10¹⁰ for a megabyte text and a 10,000-letter pattern.

The waste is this: after matching ABABA and failing on the next letter, the obvious search slides one place and re-reads letters it has already seen. But you already know what those letters are. They're the start of the pattern.

blocks.name: ds-kmp
blocks.title: Find ABABAC in a 20-letter text
blocks.goal: Run try every start to the end, then run KMP and compare.
blocks.intro: Click a pattern letter to see its failure value and what it means.

blocks.html:
A border of a string is a proper prefix that's also a suffix: aba is a border of abacaba. The prefix function pi[i] is the length of the longest border of s[0..i]. For ABABAC it's [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0]: ABABA ends with ABA, which is also how it starts.

KMP (Knuth, Morris and Pratt) keeps j, how many pattern letters currently match. For each text letter:

  1. While j > 0 and the letter doesn't match pattern[j], fall back: j = pi[j − 1]. The pi[j − 1] letters still line up, so you keep them.
  2. If it matches, j += 1. If j == m, record a match and fall back once more to look for overlapping ones.

The text pointer only moves forward. Each fall-back undoes at least one earlier step forward, so the total work is at most 2n. Building pi is the same loop run on the pattern against itself: O(m).

The Z-function is a cousin. z[i] is the length of the longest stretch starting at i that matches the start of the string. Search by building z of pattern + "\0" + text: wherever z[i] ≥ m, the pattern starts there. It's built in O(n) by remembering the rightmost match window [l, r) and reusing it, the same "don't re-read what you've seen" idea.

j becomes 3: the last 3 matched letters are also the pattern's first 3, so they're kept, and the same text letter is tried again

blocks.why: The text pointer stays put. Only j moves, to the next shorter border.

blocks.q: What's the prefix function of "aaaa"?
blocks.why: Each prefix's longest proper border is all but one of its letters.

blocks.q: Why is KMP's search O(n) even though it has a while loop inside a for loop?

opts.t: The while loop runs at most once
j goes up by at most 1 per text letter, and each fall-back lowers it, so all the fall-backs together are at most n

blocks.why: Amortised counting: you can't go down more than you went up.

blocks.q: You search with the Z-function on pattern + "\0" + text. Why the separator?

opts.t: So a match can't run past the end of the pattern into the text, which keeps every z value ≤ m

blocks.why: Without it, z values in the text could exceed m by matching across the join. The separator must be a letter in neither string.

blocks.q: s = "abcabcab". What's its shortest period?
blocks.why: The longest border is "abcab" (5), so the period is 8 − 5 = 3. s is "abc" repeated, cut off part-way.

blocks.title: Catching errors in a live log
blocks.client: An ops team whose servers stream logs in chunks of any size, who need every position where an error signature appears, even when it's split across two chunks, plus a check for heartbeat lines that repeat on a cycle
blocks.brief: Build scan.py. Logs arrive as chunks, and you can't join them all: a day's log won't fit in memory. KMP only ever needs j, the number of pattern letters matched so far, so keep j between chunks and a running position. A signature split as ERR + OR is still found. Then, for a heartbeat log, report its shortest period with the prefix function, so a monitor can tell when the cycle breaks.
blocks.why: Streaming string matchers run inside intrusion detection systems, log shippers, grep, and antivirus scanners, which see data as packets, never as one string. The prefix function's period trick finds repeating units in DNA and in compressed data.

milestones: Positions counted across the whole stream
The shortest period of a heartbeat log
stretch: Many signatures at once (look up Aho-Corasick)
Report the line number, not the position

blocks.q: Explain KMP: what a border and the prefix function are, how the search uses the table after a mismatch and after a match, why it's O(n + m), how the Z-function differs and searches, and one more problem borders solve.
blocks.a: A border of a string is a proper prefix that is also a suffix. The prefix function pi[i] is the length of the longest border of s[0..i], and it's built by carrying k, the current border length: extend it when s[i] == s[k], otherwise fall back to pi[k − 1] and try again. KMP walks the text once, keeping j, the number of pattern letters matched so far. On a mismatch with j > 0 it sets j = pi[j − 1], because those letters still line up with the start of the pattern, and retries the same text letter. On a full match it records the position and sets j = pi[m − 1], so overlapping matches are found. The text pointer never moves back, and j rises by at most 1 per letter and only falls after rising, so the search is O(n) and the table O(m). The Z-function instead stores z[i], the longest common prefix of s and s[i:], built in O(n) by reusing the rightmost match window [l, r). To search, compute z of pattern + separator + text; the pattern starts wherever z ≥ m. Borders also give the shortest period, n − pi[n − 1] (s is a repeated block when that divides n), and the shortest palindrome: the longest border of s + "#" + reversed(s).

chapters.title: Rolling hashes
chapters.tagline: Turn every substring into a number you can compare in one step
goals: Hash a string as a number in base B, modulo a big prime
Roll a window's hash forward in O(1), and get any substring's hash from prefix hashes
Search with Rabin-Karp, and know why a hash match is checked or made near-certain
Combine hashing with binary search and sets to find repeats

blocks.html:
Comparing two strings of length m takes m steps. Comparing two numbers takes one. So turn strings into numbers: read the letters as digits in base B.

hash("abc") = (a·B² + b·B + c) mod M

With a huge prime M, different strings almost never share a hash. Two things make this powerful:

  • Rolling. Slide a window one letter right: subtract the leaving letter's share (letter · Bᵐ⁻¹), multiply by B, add the new letter. O(1), however long the window.
  • Prefix hashes. Store h[i], the hash of the first i letters, and pw[i] = Bⁱ. Then any substring's hash is h[r] − h[l]·pw[r − l] (mod M), in O(1). It's chapter 4's prefix sums, for strings.

blocks.name: ds-roll
blocks.title: Find ABRAC by hashing every window
blocks.goal: Run from scratch to the end, then run rolling hash and compare.
blocks.intro: The modulus here is a tiny 61, so you'll see a collision. Real code uses a prime near 2⁶¹.

blocks.html:
Rabin-Karp search hashes the pattern once, then rolls a window along the text, comparing numbers. A hash match is either a real match or a collision. With a small M, check the letters. With M = 2⁶¹ − 1 and a fixed base, a collision is about one in 10¹⁸ per comparison, so many contest solutions skip the check. But a Codeforces "anti-hash" test can break a known, fixed base. Pick the base at random, or use two hashes, when someone could be attacking you.

Python's big integers make % MOD exact with no overflow worries. In C++ you'd use unsigned 64-bit tricks for 2⁶¹ − 1.

blocks.code:
class PrefixHash:
    def __init__(self, s):
        n = len(s)
        self.h = [0] * (n + 1)
        self.pw = [1] * (n + 1)
        for i, c in enumerate(s):
            self.h[i + 1] = (self.h[i] * BASE + ord(c)) % MOD
            self.pw[i + 1] = self.pw[i] * BASE % MOD

    def get(self, l, r):                 # hash of s[l:r]
        return (self.h[r] - self.h[l] * self.pw[r - l]) % MOD

s = "abracadabra"
ph = PrefixHash(s)
print(ph.get(0, 4) == ph.get(7, 11), s[0:4], s[7:11])
print(ph.get(0, 3) == ph.get(5, 8), s[0:3], s[5:8])
print(ph.get(0, 11) % 1000)
blocks.title: Prefix hashes: any substring in O(1)

blocks.code:
B, M = 10, 1000
h = 0
for d in [4, 7, 2]:
    h = (h * B + d) % M
print(h)
h = ((h - 4 * B ** 2) * B + 9) % M
print(h)

blocks.starter:
def rabin_karp(text, pat):
    m = len(pat)
    hp = sum(map(ord, pat))
    return [i for i in range(len(text) - m + 1) if sum(map(ord, text[i:i + 2])) == hp]

blocks.q: Two windows have the same hash. What do you know?

opts.t: They're almost certainly equal with a huge prime modulus, but a collision is possible

blocks.why: Many strings map to each hash value. With M ≈ 2⁶¹ the chance of a clash is tiny, but not zero.

blocks.q: Why is a sum of letter codes a bad hash?

opts.t: It ignores order, so "ab" and "ba" always collide

blocks.why: A polynomial hash gives each position its own power of the base, so order matters.

blocks.q: A contest's hacker sees your code uses BASE = 131 and MOD = 2⁶¹ − 1, fixed. What can they do?

opts.t: Build a test with two different strings that share a hash, breaking your answer

blocks.why: Anti-hash tests exist for known parameters. A random base chosen at run time makes them impossible to prepare.

blocks.q: h[i] is the hash of the first i letters. Which gives the hash of s[l:r]?
blocks.why: h[r] contains h[l], shifted up r − l places.

blocks.title: Copied or not?
blocks.client: A university's essay portal that compares each submission against earlier ones and flags pairs that share long runs of text
blocks.brief: Build plagiarism.py. Break each document into shingles: every run of k letters. Hash each one in O(1) with prefix hashes, giving a set of numbers per document. Two essays that share many shingles share many long runs. Report the number of shared shingles and the Jaccard similarity, |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|, which is 1 for copies and near 0 for unrelated texts.

Ignore case and punctuation

blocks.title: hash_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: same(s, queries) where each query is (a, b, L). Return a list of booleans: is s[a:a+L] == s[b:b+L]? Use prefix hashes, O(1) per query.
blocks.tests: assert same("abracadabra", [(0, 7, 4), (0, 1, 3), (1, 8, 3), (2, 2, 5)]) == [True, False, True, True]
hints: Prefix hashes and powers, then compare h[a+L] − h[a]·pw[L] with the same for b.
blocks.starter:
def same(s, queries):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def same(s, queries):
    n = len(s)
    h, pw = [0] * (n + 1), [1] * (n + 1)
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        h[i + 1] = (h[i] * BASE + ord(c)) % MOD
        pw[i + 1] = pw[i] * BASE % MOD
    get = lambda l, r: (h[r] - h[l] * pw[r - l]) % MOD
    return [get(a, a + L) == get(b, b + L) for a, b, L in queries]

blocks.q: Explain rolling hashes: how a polynomial hash is defined, how a window rolls in O(1), how prefix hashes give any substring's hash, what collisions are and how to guard against them, and two problems hashing solves.
blocks.a: A polynomial hash reads the letters as digits in base B, modulo a large prime M: hash(s) = s₀·Bᵐ⁻¹ + … + sₘ₋₁ (mod M), so order matters (a sum of letters would not). To slide a window one place, subtract the leaving letter times Bᵐ⁻¹, multiply by B, and add the new letter, which is O(1) per step. Rabin-Karp searches this way in O(n + m). Prefix hashes store h[i] for the first i letters and pw[i] = Bⁱ, and the hash of s[l:r] is h[r] − h[l]·pw[r − l] mod M, so any two substrings compare in O(1). Different strings can share a hash (a collision). With M near 2⁶¹ that's about a 1 in 10¹⁸ chance per comparison. Guard against it by confirming matches by slicing, using two hashes, or picking a random base so anti-hash tests can't be prepared. Hashing finds the longest duplicate substring (binary search on the length, with a set of window hashes), finds repeated DNA windows, and measures document similarity with shingles and Jaccard.

chapters.title: Suffix arrays
chapters.tagline: Sort every suffix once, and a whole family of string questions becomes a scan
goals: Build a suffix array by prefix doubling, comparing pairs of ranks instead of strings
Build the LCP array with Kasai's algorithm in O(n)
Count distinct substrings, and find the longest repeated and longest common substring
Find every occurrence of a pattern by binary searching the suffix array

blocks.html:
The suffixes of banana are banana, anana, nana, ana, na, a. Sort them and write down where each one starts:

rankstartsuffix
05a
13ana
21anana
30banana
44na
52nana

The suffix array is that list of starts: [5, 3, 1, 0, 4, 2]. It's just n numbers, but every substring of the text is a prefix of some suffix, so in this sorted list all copies of any substring sit next to each other. That turns searching, counting and comparing into binary searches and scans.

Sorting the suffixes as strings is slow: a comparison can read a long way before two suffixes differ, n letters on text like abab….

blocks.name: ds-suffix
blocks.title: Sort the 16 suffixes of abababababababab
blocks.goal: Step through sort whole strings, then prefix doubling, and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Each row is a suffix. Blue letters are the part the rows are already sorted by.

blocks.html:
Prefix doubling sorts by the first 1 letter, then 2, then 4, then 8. The trick: once you know the rank of every suffix's first k letters, the first 2k letters of suffix i are two ranks side by side, (rank[i], rank[i + k]). A suffix too short for its second half uses −1, which sorts before everything. Sort by that pair, give equal pairs equal ranks, double k, and stop when all ranks differ. That's at most log n rounds, each a sort of n small tuples: O(n log² n), and fast in Python because tuples are compared in C.

Next to it sits the LCP array: lcp[r] is the length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes at ranks r − 1 and r. Kasai's algorithm builds it in O(n) by visiting suffixes in text order: if suffix i shares h letters with its neighbour, suffix i + 1 shares at least h − 1 with its own, so h never drops by more than 1 per step.

blocks.title: Suffix array by prefix doubling, and Kasai's LCP

blocks.code:
s = "abab"
print(sorted(range(len(s)), key=lambda i: s[i:]))

blocks.q: In a suffix array, where are all the occurrences of the substring "ana" in "banana"?

opts.t: In one block of neighbours: every suffix that starts with "ana" sorts together

blocks.why: Ranks 1 and 2 (starts 3 and 1). That's what makes binary search work.

blocks.q: How much memory does a suffix array use for a text of n letters?
blocks.why: It stores starts, not suffixes. The text itself holds the letters.

blocks.q: How many rounds does prefix doubling need at most?

opts.t: About log₂ n, since the sorted length doubles each round

blocks.why: After round t, suffixes are sorted by their first 2ᵗ letters. Once that's ≥ n, all ranks differ.

blocks.q: Why does Kasai's algorithm run in O(n)?

opts.t: h falls by at most 1 per step and can never exceed n, so it rises at most 2n times in total

blocks.why: The same amortised argument as KMP's fall-backs.

blocks.q: s has 10 letters and its LCP array sums to 12. How many distinct substrings does it have?
blocks.why: 10·11/2 = 55 substrings with repeats, minus the 12 that repeat an earlier one.

sections.title: Real-world project: a code search index

blocks.title: Find every match in a big codebase
blocks.client: A developer tool that searches a 50,000-letter codebase for any snippet the user types, instantly and as many times as they like
blocks.brief: Build codesearch.py. Build the suffix array of the text once. Every occurrence of a query sits in one block of neighbouring suffixes, so two binary searches find it: the first suffix whose first m letters are ≥ the query, and the first one whose first m letters are > it. Each binary search compares m letters about log n times: O(m log n) per query, whatever the text size. Return the positions in text order, or just the count.
blocks.why: Suffix arrays (and their compressed cousins, FM-indexes) power genome aligners like BWA and Bowtie, full-text search in tools like zoekt, and data compression (the Burrows-Wheeler transform behind bzip2).

blocks.q: Explain suffix arrays: what the array and the LCP array hold, how prefix doubling builds the array and why a comparison is O(1), how Kasai builds LCP in O(n), and three problems they solve.
blocks.a: The suffix array lists the start positions of all suffixes in sorted order. Every substring is a prefix of some suffix, so all copies of a substring sit in one block of neighbours. Prefix doubling sorts by the first 1, 2, 4… letters. Once each suffix's rank by its first k letters is known, its first 2k letters are the pair (rank[i], rank[i + k]), with −1 for a missing half so it sorts before every real rank (ranks themselves start at 0). Sorting those pairs and re-ranking takes log n rounds, O(n log² n) in all, and each comparison is two small numbers rather than a walk along strings. The LCP array holds the common-prefix length of each pair of neighbouring suffixes. Kasai builds it in O(n) by visiting suffixes in text order and carrying h, which drops by at most 1 per step. Uses: the number of distinct substrings is n(n+1)/2 − sum(lcp); the longest repeat is the largest LCP value; the longest common substring of a and b is the largest LCP between neighbours from different sides of a + separator + b; and finding every occurrence of a pattern takes two binary searches over the suffix array, O(m log n) each.

chapters.title: Strongly connected components
chapters.tagline: Group a one-way graph into places that can all reach each other, in two passes
goals: Say what a strongly connected component is, and why the naive test costs n searches
Write Kosaraju's algorithm with two iterative DFS passes, O(n + m)
Shrink the graph to its components (the condensation, always a DAG) and run DP on it
Count the sources and sinks of the condensation to answer "how many roads to add?"
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import Counter

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

def lcg(n, seed, mx):
    out, x = [], seed
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2 ** 31
        out.append(x % mx)
    return out

def digraph(n, m, seed):
    """About m random one-way edges (a, b) on nodes 0..n-1, no self-loops."""
    g = [x * n // 10 ** 9 for x in lcg(2 * m, seed, 10 ** 9)]
    return [(g[2 * i], g[2 * i + 1]) for i in range(m) if g[2 * i] != g[2 * i + 1]]

sections.title: Who can reach whom, and back

blocks.html:
In a one-way graph (links on the web, follows on a social network, calls between functions, one-way streets), u can reach v without v reaching u. A strongly connected component (SCC) is a largest group in which every node can reach every other and come back. Every node belongs to exactly one SCC, possibly on its own.

The obvious way: search from every node, then group u and v together when each reaches the other. That's n searches, O(n·(n + m)): 10¹⁰ for a graph of 10⁵ nodes.

blocks.name: ds-scc
blocks.title: Twelve places and their one-way roads
blocks.goal: Run search from every place to the end, then run Kosaraju, two passes and compare.
blocks.intro: The small block on each road sits near the end it points to.

blocks.html:
Kosaraju's algorithm needs only two searches over the whole graph:

  1. Pass 1. DFS over the graph, starting a new search from every unvisited node. Write each node down when it finishes (all its roads are done).
  2. Pass 2. Reverse every edge. Go through the nodes from last finished to first; each one not yet labelled starts a search on the reversed graph, and everything that search reaches is one SCC.

Why pass 2 can't leak: the last node to finish sits in a "source" group, with no roads coming in from other unvisited groups. Reversed, the roads leaving its group now point in, so a backward search stays home. Its group is then removed, and the next latest finisher is a source of what's left.

A bonus: SCCs come out in topological order. Shrink each one to a single node (the condensation), and every edge between groups goes from a lower group number to a higher one. The condensation never has a cycle, because a cycle of groups would be one bigger group. So any DAG technique (chapter 21's topological order, chapter 28's DP) now works on graphs with cycles.

For 10⁵ nodes, Python's recursion limit makes recursive DFS crash, so both passes use an explicit stack.

blocks.code:
def scc(n, edges):
    out = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    inn = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for a, b in edges:
        out[a].append(b)
        inn[b].append(a)
    seen, order = [False] * n, []
    for s in range(n):                      # pass 1: finishing order
        if seen[s]:
            continue
        seen[s] = True
        st = [(s, 0)]
        while st:
            x, i = st[-1]
            if i < len(out[x]):
                st[-1] = (x, i + 1)
                y = out[x][i]
                if not seen[y]:
                    seen[y] = True
                    st.append((y, 0))
            else:
                st.pop()
                order.append(x)
    comp, c = [-1] * n, 0
    for s in reversed(order):               # pass 2: reversed edges
        if comp[s] != -1:
            continue
        comp[s] = c
        st = [s]
        while st:
            x = st.pop()
            for y in inn[x]:
                if comp[y] == -1:
                    comp[y] = c
                    st.append(y)
        c += 1
    return comp

print(scc(6, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 4)]))
comp = scc(100000, digraph(100000, 120000, 3))
sizes = Counter(comp)
print(len(sizes), "groups, the biggest has", max(sizes.values()))

blocks.q: Explain strongly connected components: what one is, how Kosaraju's two passes find them and why pass 2 can't leak between groups, what the condensation is and why it's a DAG, and two problems that use it.
blocks.a: A strongly connected component is a largest set of nodes in a directed graph where every node can reach every other, and every node is in exactly one. Testing each pair needs a search from every node, O(n(n + m)). Kosaraju does two DFS passes, O(n + m). Pass 1 runs DFS over the whole graph and records nodes in the order they finish. Pass 2 reverses every edge and processes nodes from the last finisher to the first, and each search from an unlabelled node labels exactly one SCC. The last finisher lies in a source group of the remaining graph, so after reversal every edge leaving that group points into it, or into a group already labelled, and the search stays inside. Both passes use an explicit stack to avoid recursion limits. The condensation shrinks each SCC to one node. It's a DAG, because a cycle of groups would merge them into one, and Kosaraju's labels come out in topological order. Uses: Checkposts (one cheapest post per SCC, multiplying the ways), Coin Collector (sum the coins in each SCC, then a longest-path DP on the DAG), and the fewest edges to make a graph strongly connected, max(sources, sinks), or 0 for a single group.

chapters.title: Bridges and articulation points
chapters.tagline: Find every single point of failure in one depth-first search
goals: Define disc and low for every node of a DFS tree
Find bridges (low[child] > disc[parent]) and articulation points (low[child] ≥ disc[parent], with a special case for the root)
Skip the parent edge, not the parent node, so parallel edges are handled
Shrink 2-edge-connected blocks into a tree and count the edges needed to remove every bridge

blocks.html:
In a network of two-way links (roads, power lines, network cables), a bridge is a link whose loss splits the network, and an articulation point (cut vertex) is a node whose loss does. Finding them tells you where to add redundancy.

The obvious way: remove each edge, search, see if everything is still reachable. That's m searches, O(m·(n + m)), far too slow for 10⁵ roads.

blocks.name: ds-bridges
blocks.title: Twelve towns and fifteen roads
blocks.goal: Run close each road to the end, then run Tarjan's low-link and compare.
blocks.intro: In Tarjan's mode, each town shows town · disc/low.

blocks.html:
Tarjan's low-link runs one DFS and gives every node two numbers:

  • disc[v]: the time the search first reached v (0, 1, 2…).
  • low[v]: the smallest disc that v's part of the tree can reach using tree edges downwards plus one back edge (an edge to a node already visited).

When the search returns from child c to parent p, set low[p] = min(low[p], low[c]), and test:

  • Bridge. Edge p–c is a bridge when low[c] > disc[p]: nothing in c's subtree can get back to p or above without that edge.
  • Articulation point. A non-root p is a cut vertex when some child has low[c] ≥ disc[p]: that subtree can reach p, but not above it, so removing p strands it. The root is a cut vertex only when it has two or more DFS children.

Two traps. Skip the edge you came in on by its id, not by "is it my parent?": two parallel roads between the same towns mean neither is a bridge, and skipping by node would miss the second one. And use an explicit stack, because 10⁵ nodes overflow Python's recursion.

blocks.a: One DFS gives every node disc, the time it was first reached, and low, the smallest disc its subtree can reach using tree edges downwards plus one back edge. When the search returns from child c to parent p, set low[p] = min(low[p], low[c]); a back edge to an already-visited w sets low[v] = min(low[v], disc[w]). chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import deque

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

def lcg(n, seed, mx):
    out, x = [], seed
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2 ** 31
        out.append(x % mx)
    return out

def network(n, m, seed, cmax):
    """About m random pipes (a, b, capacity 1..cmax) on nodes 0..n-1."""
    g = [x * n // 10 ** 9 for x in lcg(2 * m, seed, 10 ** 9)]
    c = lcg(m, seed + 1, cmax)
    return [(g[2 * i], g[2 * i + 1], c[i] + 1) for i in range(m) if g[2 * i] != g[2 * i + 1]]

TRAP = [(0, 1, 2), (1, 2, 2), (1, 4, 2), (0, 2, 2), (2, 4, 2), (0, 3, 1), (3, 4, 1)]   # s=0 a=1 b=2 c=3 t=4

blocks.html:
A flow network is a directed graph where each edge has a capacity, with a source s and a sink t. A flow sends an amount along each edge, at most its capacity, and at every node except s and t what comes in equals what goes out. The question: what's the most that can get from s to t?

It looks like water in pipes, but it models much more: data through a network, trucks along roads, people assigned to jobs (next chapter), and even "which pixels are foreground?" in image editing.

The obvious method: find any path from s to t with room on every edge, push as much as the tightest edge allows, and repeat. It can get stuck below the best answer.

blocks.name: ds-flow
blocks.title: Send as much as possible from s to t
blocks.goal: Run fill any path, no undo to the end, then run with undo edges and compare the totals.
blocks.intro: Each pipe shows flow/capacity. Watch what the second path does to the middle pipe.

blocks.html:
The fix is the residual graph. For every edge a → b carrying flow f, add an undo edge b → a with room f. A later path may push flow along it, which cancels flow that went a → b and reroutes it. With undo edges, no path left really means maximum. That's Ford-Fulkerson.

Two facts make it a tool you can trust:

  • Edmonds-Karp. Pick each path by BFS (fewest edges), and the number of rounds is at most O(n·m), so O(n·m²) in all, however big the capacities. In practice it's much faster.
  • Max-flow min-cut. When it stops, let S be everything still reachable from s in the residual graph. Every edge from S to the rest is full, and every edge back into S is empty. So the flow equals the total capacity of those edges, a cut, and no cut can be smaller. The bottleneck of a network is exactly as big as its best flow.

Store edges in pairs (edge e and its undo edge e ^ 1) so pushing flow is two list updates.

blocks.code:
class Flow:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n, self.adj, self.to, self.cap = n, [[] for _ in range(n)], [], []

    def add(self, a, b, c):
        self.adj[a].append(len(self.to)); self.to.append(b); self.cap.append(c)
        self.adj[b].append(len(self.to)); self.to.append(a); self.cap.append(0)   # undo edge

    def max_flow(self, s, t):
        total = 0
        while True:
            prev = [-1] * self.n
            prev[s] = -2
            q = deque([s])
            while q and prev[t] == -1:                  # BFS: shortest path with room
                v = q.popleft()
                for e in self.adj[v]:
                    w = self.to[e]
                    if self.cap[e] > 0 and prev[w] == -1:
                        prev[w] = e
                        q.append(w)
            if prev[t] == -1:
                return total
            push, v = float("inf"), t
            while v != s:                               # the bottleneck
                e = prev[v]
                push = min(push, self.cap[e])
                v = self.to[e ^ 1]
            v = t
            while v != s:                               # push it, and open the undo edges
                e = prev[v]
                self.cap[e] -= push
                self.cap[e ^ 1] += push
                v = self.to[e ^ 1]
            total += push

f = Flow(5)
for a, b, c in TRAP:
    f.add(a, b, c)
print(f.max_flow(0, 4))

blocks.q: Why does the greedy "fill any path" method fail?

opts.t: An early path can take a bad route and block others, and without undo edges it can never take that back

blocks.why: Undo edges let a later path reroute earlier flow.

blocks.q: After max flow, which edges form a minimum cut?

opts.t: Edges from the set reachable from s in the residual graph to the rest
The edges on the last path

blocks.why: Many edges can be full without being in the cut. Reachability in the residual graph picks out the bottleneck.

blocks.q: You have three warehouses and two cities. How do you run a single-source max flow?

opts.t: Run it six times and add up
Add a super source joined to each warehouse and a super sink joined from each city, with huge capacities
Merge the cities into one node by deleting edges

blocks.why: One extra node on each side turns many sources and sinks into one of each.

blocks.q: Edmonds-Karp picks augmenting paths by BFS. Why not DFS?

opts.t: With DFS the number of rounds can depend on the capacities (huge ones mean huge numbers of rounds); BFS bounds it by O(n·m)

blocks.why: Shortest paths first guarantee a bound that doesn't depend on how big the numbers are.

blocks.solution:
def throughput(n, roads, warehouses, cities):
    S, T = n, n + 1
    edges = list(roads) + [(S, w, 10 ** 9) for w in warehouses] + [(c, T, 10 ** 9) for c in cities]
    N = n + 2
    adj, to, cap = [[] for _ in range(N)], [], []
    for a, b, c in edges:
        adj[a].append(len(to)); to.append(b); cap.append(c)
        adj[b].append(len(to)); to.append(a); cap.append(0)
    total = 0
    while True:
        prev = [-1] * N
        prev[S] = -2
        q = deque([S])
        while q and prev[T] == -1:
            v = q.popleft()
            for e in adj[v]:
                w = to[e]
                if cap[e] > 0 and prev[w] == -1:
                    prev[w] = e
                    q.append(w)
        if prev[T] == -1:
            return total
        push, v = float("inf"), T
        while v != S:
            e = prev[v]
            push = min(push, cap[e])
            v = to[e ^ 1]
        v = T
        while v != S:
            e = prev[v]
            cap[e] -= push
            cap[e ^ 1] += push
            v = to[e ^ 1]
        total += push

blocks.solution:
def bottlenecks(n, roads, warehouses, cities):
    S, T = n, n + 1
    edges = list(roads) + [(S, w, 10 ** 9) for w in warehouses] + [(c, T, 10 ** 9) for c in cities]
    N = n + 2
    adj, to, cap = [[] for _ in range(N)], [], []
    for a, b, c in edges:
        adj[a].append(len(to)); to.append(b); cap.append(c)
        adj[b].append(len(to)); to.append(a); cap.append(0)
    while True:
        prev = [-1] * N
        prev[S] = -2
        q = deque([S])
        while q and prev[T] == -1:
            v = q.popleft()
            for e in adj[v]:
                w = to[e]
                if cap[e] > 0 and prev[w] == -1:
                    prev[w] = e
                    q.append(w)
        if prev[T] == -1:
            break
        push, v = float("inf"), T
        while v != S:
            e = prev[v]
            push = min(push, cap[e])
            v = to[e ^ 1]
        v = T
        while v != S:
            e = prev[v]
            cap[e] -= push
            cap[e ^ 1] += push
            v = to[e ^ 1]
    seen = [False] * N
    seen[S] = True
    st = [S]
    while st:
        v = st.pop()
        for e in adj[v]:
            if cap[e] > 0 and not seen[to[e]]:
                seen[to[e]] = True
                st.append(to[e])
    return [i for i, (a, b, c) in enumerate(roads) if seen[a] and not seen[b]]

blocks.q: Explain maximum flow: what a flow network and a flow are, why greedy paths get stuck and how residual edges fix it, how Edmonds-Karp works and its bound, what the max-flow min-cut theorem says and how to read the cut, and how to handle many sources and sinks.
blocks.a: A flow network is a directed graph with a capacity on each edge, a source s and a sink t. A flow puts an amount on each edge, at most its capacity, and conserves flow at every node except s and t. The goal is to maximise what leaves s. Repeatedly filling any path that has room can get stuck, because an early path may block better routes. The residual graph adds, for every edge carrying f, an undo edge in the opposite direction with room f, so a later augmenting path can cancel and reroute earlier flow. With undo edges, "no augmenting path" means the flow is maximum (Ford-Fulkerson). Edmonds-Karp chooses each path by BFS (fewest edges), which bounds the number of rounds by O(n·m) whatever the capacities, so O(n·m²) in all. Storing each edge next to its partner (e and e ^ 1) makes a push two list updates. The max-flow min-cut theorem says the maximum flow equals the smallest total capacity of edges whose removal separates s from t. Read the cut by finding everything reachable from s in the final residual graph: the edges leaving that set are full and form a minimum cut. For many sources or sinks, add a super source with huge-capacity edges to each source and a super sink from each sink. Unit capacities count link-disjoint paths.

chapters.title: Bipartite matching
chapters.tagline: Pair up two groups as fully as possible by shuffling along augmenting paths
goals: Recognise a bipartite matching problem (workers and jobs, rows and columns, black and white cells)
Find augmenting paths, and know why a matching with none is maximum
Write Kuhn's algorithm, O(V·E), and reset the visited marks for each new start
Use König's theorem: in a bipartite graph, the smallest vertex cover equals the largest matching
chapters.prelude:
import sys
import time
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

def lcg(n, seed, mx):
    out, x = [], seed
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2 ** 31
        out.append(x % mx)
    return out

def bigraph(nl, nr, m, seed):
    """adj[left] = the right-side nodes it may be paired with, about m random lines."""
    g = [x / 10 ** 9 for x in lcg(2 * m, seed, 10 ** 9)]
    adj = [[] for _ in range(nl)]
    for i in range(m):
        a, b = int(g[2 * i] * nl), int(g[2 * i + 1] * nr)
        if b not in adj[a]:
            adj[a].append(b)
    return adj

ADJ = [[0, 1], [0], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 5], [4, 5]]   # worker -> jobs they can do

blocks.html:
A graph is bipartite when its nodes split into two sides and every edge crosses between them: workers and the jobs they can do, students and project slots, rows and columns of a grid. A matching picks edges with no shared endpoint (each worker gets at most one job, each job at most one worker). The goal is a maximum matching: as many pairs as possible.

The obvious way, giving each worker the first free job, gets stuck:

blocks.name: ds-match
blocks.title: Six workers, six jobs
blocks.goal: Run first free job to the end, then run augmenting paths and compare.
blocks.intro: Lines show who can do what. Green lines are the current matching.

blocks.html:
The fix is an augmenting path: start at a free worker, go to a job they can do; if a worker holds it, go to that worker and on to another job they can do; keep alternating until you reach a free job. Flip every line on the path (matched becomes unmatched and the other way round) and the matching grows by one, with nobody losing a job.

Berge's theorem says a matching is maximum exactly when no augmenting path exists. So:

Kuhn's algorithm. For each worker, run a DFS try_kuhn(v): for each job j of v not yet visited in this search, mark it; if j is free, or its holder can find another job by try_kuhn, give j to v. That's O(V·E) in the worst case and quick in practice. (Hopcroft-Karp finds many shortest paths per round for O(E·√V), and max flow with unit capacities does the same job, chapter 53.)

König's theorem gives a second tool: in a bipartite graph, the fewest nodes that touch every edge (a vertex cover) is exactly the size of a maximum matching. "Fewest rows and columns that cover every marked cell" is a matching question in disguise.

blocks.q: When is a matching maximum?

opts.t: When every left node is matched
When there's no augmenting path (Berge's theorem)

blocks.why: A matching can be maximum with nodes left over, if the graph simply doesn't allow more.

blocks.q: Why must seen be reset for each new worker in Kuhn's algorithm?

opts.t: A job explored in an earlier failed or finished search may be reachable in a different way now; stale marks hide it

blocks.why: Inside one search the marks stop loops. Across searches they block valid paths.

blocks.q: A bipartite graph has a maximum matching of size 7. What's the smallest number of nodes that touch every edge?
blocks.why: In bipartite graphs, minimum vertex cover = maximum matching. (In general graphs that's not true.)

blocks.q: How can max flow solve bipartite matching?

opts.t: Source → every left node (capacity 1), left → right along each line (1), every right node → sink (1); the max flow is the matching size

blocks.why: Each unit of flow is one pair, and the capacities stop anyone being used twice.

blocks.title: interns_who_goes_where
blocks.prompt: Write assignment(prefs, seats): a list where entry i is the team intern i joins, or -1. It must place the maximum number, never overfill a team, and only use teams the intern accepts.
blocks.tests:
def check(prefs, seats, a, best):
    assert len(a) == len(prefs)
    assert sum(1 for t in a if t != -1) == best, "place as many as possible"
    for i, t in enumerate(a):
        assert t == -1 or t in prefs[i], "only teams the intern accepts"
    for t, k in enumerate(seats):
        assert a.count(t) <= k, "never overfill a team"
check([[0, 1], [0]], [1, 1], assignment([[0, 1], [0]], [1, 1]), 2)
check([[0], [0], [1], [0, 1]], [2, 1], assignment([[0], [0], [1], [0, 1]], [2, 1]), 3)
g = lcg(200, 9, 1000)
prefs = [[g[2 * i + k] * 60 // 1000 for k in range(2)] for i in range(100)]
seats = [1 + x * 3 // 1000 for x in lcg(60, 10, 1000)]
check(prefs, seats, assignment(prefs, seats), 96)

blocks.q: Explain bipartite matching: what a matching and an augmenting path are, Berge's theorem, how Kuhn's algorithm works and why seen is reset for each start, its cost, and König's theorem with an example.
blocks.a: In a bipartite graph every edge crosses between two sides. A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoint, and a maximum matching has as many edges as possible. Greedily taking the first free partner can get stuck. An augmenting path starts at a free left node and alternates unmatched and matched edges until it reaches a free right node. Flipping every edge on it adds one pair and unmatches nobody. Berge's theorem: a matching is maximum exactly when no augmenting path exists. Kuhn's algorithm runs a DFS try_kuhn(v) for each left node: for each partner j not seen in this search, mark it, and if j is free or its owner can be rehoused by a recursive try_kuhn, give j to v. The marks stop loops within one search. They must be fresh for each new start, because stale marks from earlier searches block valid paths. Cost O(V·E); Hopcroft-Karp is O(E·√V), and unit-capacity max flow also works. König's theorem: in a bipartite graph, the minimum vertex cover equals the maximum matching. So the fewest rows and columns covering every marked cell is a matching between rows and columns, and dominoes on a grid are a matching between black and white cells.
